speechtext: Mr. J. E. ARMSTRONG (East Lambton) moved the second reading of Bill No. 3, to amend the Railway Act. He said: This Bill will, I believe, be of great benefit to producers and shippers in western and eastern Canada. It calls for the placing of vessels on our inland waters under the control of the Railway Commission. The transportation problem is one of the most important with which Canada has to deal. We have a vast territory and a small population. Our lines of communication in many instances have been built in advance of the needs of the districts through which they run. With the most wonderful water transportation facilities in the world and with a

people who are ready and willing to develop these advantages, we have the duty imposed upon us of assisting this development.
In Europe artificial and natural waterways are developed to an enormous extent. The great bulk of the grain and grain products are never carried by rail. The port which has behind it a navigable stream or canal has a wonderful advantage over its competitor that depends entirely upon railway transportation. When the Welland canal is completed the Canadian Government will have expended since Confederation $350,000,000 in developing our waterways. This is an enormous sum of money, and it is the duty of Parliament -to sui'round the people who have been so generous, with legislation that will mean every safeguard in the transportation of our products both east and west. This expenditure is increasing year by year, and the charges of maintenance and operation are being borne by the people. We have great fleets of dredges, ice breakers, and barges, that are constantly assisting navigation, and practically all these advantages are free to the vessel-owners, who are not compelled to make any sacrifices for them. Notwithstanding this enormous outlay freight rates keep steadily increasing.
A commission, - appointed by the Saskatchewan Government two years ago for the purpose of investigating the freight rates from the producers in Saskatchewan to the Liverpool markets, made some startling statements. One statement was that the lake-carriers' charges have doubled since 1909. If hon. members will look at the report placed in their hands by the Joint Commission appointed by the Senate and the House of Commons for the purpose of investigating the consolidation of the Railway Act, they will find on the last page of it a statement made by the Deputy Minister of Railways and Canals which practically supports the statement made by the Saskatchewan Commission. If this statement is correct, and I have no reason to doubt that it is correct, then, it is the duty of this Parliament to surround the producers in western Canada with such legislation that they may receive a reasonable service for a reasonable rate.
The Liverpool mark d, we know, regulates the price of grain products for the whole world. Every dollar that we add to the cost of transportation of our products to that market means that the producer in Canada receives one dollar less. Another statement made by the commission appointed by the Saskatchewan government 
was that our ocean freight rates have increased since 1909 to an enormous extent. They say that, while in 1909 the cost of transporting a thousand bushels of grain from the port of Montreal to Liverpool was only $40, the present charge for that service is no less than $75. They say that the grain of Canada costs more per ton delivered to the Liverpool market than does the grain of any other country in the world. If that be true, the^ sooner we adopt the Bill which I have presented to the House and allow the Railway Commission to deal v ith this question the better it will be for the producers of Canada. Is it possible that grain can be collected at the ports of the Argentine Republic with its territory very similar to our own, and transported a distance of about 5,000 miles across the ocean, practically double the distance that our grain has to be transported, and delivered in Liverpool at a less cost than we have to pay with all our splendid facilities? Is it possible that grain can be carried from Australia and New Zealand, 12,000 miles from Liverpool, at a less cost than from Canada?
The governments of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta have built hundreds of elevators in these western provinces. This Government, also, has built large elevators in Saskatoon and Moosejaw, and others are in course of construction. The Railway Commission has control of freight rates from the time the grain leaves the producer until it arrives at Port Arthur or Fort William. But there it is handed over to the vessel owner who is free to make any charge he pleases, to enter into any arrangement he wishes. We have appointed a Grain Commission to assist the producers in the West to secure a fair and adequate return for their efforts. But after we have expended the 'enormous sums I have already stated on the maintenance and improvements of our inland waterways, the vesselmen can take that grain, carry it where they please, and charge what they please without restriction.
The building of elevators at our ports has materially assisted in the handling of gram. Montreal has elevators with capacity of about nine million bushels. And just a word with regard to the port of Montreal, because men who are interested in the carrying of grain on our inland waters have placed some definite statements on that subject before the committee that had this Bill under consideration. They stated that last season vessels had to remain in the port of Mont-

real, ten, fifteen and even twenty days before they could be unloaded. They said that the elevators of the Montreal Harbour Commissioners at the port of Montreal in 1907 only handled a little over a million bushels of grain, while owing to their greatly increased elevator capacity they were able last year to handle sixty-two million bushels. That is an enormous increase. But the president of the Marine Association and others declare that the port of Montreal is not yet capable of taking care of the grain that comes to that port. If that be the case, it is up to this Parliament, it is up to the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal, to put forth every effort to remedy that state of affairs. Those of you who will read the book that has been placed in your hands by the Gazette Publishing Company of Montreal during the last few weeks, a book for which that concern deserves a great deal of credit, will learn that vessels containing 1,500,000 bushels of grain after reaching the port of Montreal could not be accommodated there, and were compelled to return to Buffalo to unload their grain rather than lose the twenty days or more of waiting in Montreal harbour during the two months when there was a blockade in that port. This is another reason why the Railway Commissioners should have control over our shipping rates. They should be able to force the speculators who hold up grain in the port of Montreal to send that grain forward; and should be able also to provide sufficient elevator capacity for the handling of our products from the West.
It is estimated that when the Welland canal is completed we shall save one cent a bushel in cost of transportation. But if this Parliament will not surround the producer with such legislative protection as I am proposing, the whole of that saving will go, not to the producers but to the transportation interests.
One great difficulty is that grain is held in Montreal by speculators, and the Harbour Commissioners seem to be powerless to force these men to export it.
The port of Buffalo handles about 150,000,000 bushels of wheat per annum. The bulk of that wheat is not exported, but is for consumption in the United States.
The carrying trade of this country, especially water transportation, is capable of wonderful development; Canada is only at the beginning of the development -of her industries. It has been stated that only two per cent of the arable land in Alberta is under cultivation, and it has also
been stated by members of this House that only ten per cent of the arable land in Saskatchewan is under cultivation. I remember listening to a speech made by a former minister of the province of Manitoba, during the course of which he said that the province of Manitoba-then without its increased area-was capable of producing at least 500,000,000 bushels of wheat in addition to other grains. I have no reason to doubt that assertion. In the face of these facts, is it not wise that we should enact such legislation as I am proposing, in order that we may assist the western producer as much as possible?
I know that the Government have received many urgent requests to defeat this legislation. I understand that this very day we have men here representing the shipping interests who assert that every member of the Joint Commission of the House of Commons and the . Senate are opposed to this Bill. I wish to say to these visiting gentlemen that that assertion is' untrue. I feel confident that not half a dozen members of the committee will oppose this legislation, and I feel sure that it is not too much for the producers to ask that their interests be protected, and that whatever is done by the vessel men be done in the interests of the public.
There are 8,500 vessels registered in Canada, and the Department of Marine and Fisheries report that 42,500 men and boys are working on those vessels. The Department of Railways and Canals reports that during 1913 the total tonnage passing through American and Canadian canals was 79,000,000 tons, and that 55 per cent of that was carried through Canadian canals. The people of Canada furnish every means to assist transportation on our inland waters, and they protect the marine interests against foreign shipping. Our coast regulations give Canadian vessels advantage over vessels of other countries ; in other words, we retain for our vessel owners the exclusive right to enjoy the coasting privileges. All vessels owned, constructed or operated in connection with the railway system in Canada are compelled to file their tolls, rates and tariff arrangements with the Board of Railway Commissioners, and the Railway Commission have absolute control over those arrangements. Only a small proportion of the vessels on our inland waters come under the jurisdiction of the Railway Board. If the ships carrying freight on our inland waters and connected with our railways are compelled to come under the jurisdiction of the

Board of Bailway Commissioners, what reason can be given why other vessels should not be willing to come under that same jurisdiction? The railway men have not 'complained because (they have been placed under the jurisdiction of the Board of Bailway Commissioners, and there is no reason why the vessel men should not be fairly treated by the Board if they were placed under their control.
This Bill simply asks that all other vessels plying between any port or place in Canada to other ports in Canada and handling produce of any kind in Canada shall be considered common carriers and come under the jurisdiction of the Bailway Commission. The vessel men protest strongly against being placed under the jurisdiction of the board, and assert that it will result in increased freight rates and lack of competition. Increased freight rates? Is it possible that these men object to increased freight rates. Increased freight rates means increased profits for these men. I feel that I am justified in making the assertion that there is mighty little competition on our inland waters to-day. I want to make use of a statement made before'the joint committee by Mr. Henderson, Chairman of the Marine Association, in which he said that 90 per cent of the vessels on our inland waters are under the control of the Marine Association. He also said that with regard to rates, charges tolls and agreements they had no combination. But it seems very strange that these men are ready and willing to organize and band themselves together, unless it be for their own mutual benefit.
Bemember that we must take into consideration not only the large shippers of grain and products from western Canada, but the small manufacturer; the small producer from eastern Canada who is anxious to ship his goods to the West to compete with similar products coming in from the united States. These men are seriously handicapped because of the restrictions surrounding them and forced upon them by the vessel owners. I am informed that unless *some definite action is taken by this Government during the present session, increased freight rates will be charged to the shippers both in the East and in the West. I hope that the Government will see to it, therefore, that this Bill becomes law and that a reasonable service and reasonable rates are granted to shippers, both east and west. It cannot with justice be said that the Bailway Commission

has not the right to control in this matter, and that the Marine and Fisheries Department of Canada is likely to interfere. I have made a thorough investigation into this pha£e of the matter, and I have the most definite assurance from the best legal advisers-men who are thoroughly posted in regard to the marine laws of Canada-that nothing can interfere with this legislation if it once becomes law. I, therefore, respectfully urge the Government to place this legislation on the statute book at the earliest possible moment giving to the Bailway Commission control of all freight charges, and tariff agreements made by vessel men. By doing this they will enable manufacturers and producers to do business on a basis of reasonable service. They will make the boat owners liable for any failure in their duty. The Board will fix penalties, and provide for fair and equitable treatment of all interests using our navigable waters. Vessel men giving service need not fear this legislation; those who do not give such service should be compelled to do so.

speechtext:
Most assuredly.
There is another clause dealing with certain

25o
privileges granted by railway companies to shippers and manufacturers in the eastern provinces especially. I have received petitions and letters from numerous shippers and manufacturers who feel that they are seriously handicapped by the privileges which are being granted to other shippers and manufacturers in the eastern provinces, and of which they cannot take advantage. For instance, before the joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons, it was shown that the Board of Trade of Toronto had formulated several objections to the privileges granted by railway companies to millers and speculators whereby large quantities of grain are stored in cars at Port Arthur or Fort William or in Winnipeg, the rolling stock which should be placed at the disposal of the producers in our western country being thereby tied up and the advantage which should accrue to the producers
4 p.m. through the handling of their grain seriously lessened. I might also refer to the privileges granted to real estate speculators, particularly in western towns, who are also interested in railway companies who have been able to induce the railways to pass by communities which are thickly settled and to establish town-sites at points where there is no reason or justification for their establishment. The Board of Railway Commissioners have distinctly stated time and again that they have no control over the privileges granted by the railway corporations in this respect. This clause merely provides that all these privileges shall come under the jurisdiction of the Railway Board. Questions such as cartage should also come under their jurisdiction. I am satisfied that the matters which I have laid before the House call for a remedy, and I believe that the remedy is to be found in the Bill that I am now proposing. There is not a farmers' organization in western Canada that will not support this Bill nor is there a fruit or vegetable growers' .association in eastern Canada that will not be enthusiastically for it. Boards of trade, shippers and manufacturers in different parts of our country have been calling for just such legislation as this, and I am confident that it is tlje duty of the Government to place it on the statute book at the earliest possible moment.

maintopic: FIRST CANADIAN CONTINGENT- SUPPLY OF CARTRIDGES.
speechtext:
I am glad the hon. gentleman has brought forward this Bill. Most members will agree that it is a very necessary one. The principle was discussed and received very general acceptance in this
House a year ago. There is absolutely no reason why the' steamship companies should not come under the Board of Railway Commissioners. No decision of the Railway Board has ever been challenged as unfair. The railway companies themselves are satisfied with the board. I was told by one of the biggest railway men in Canada about two years ago that if they had a choice they would not go hack to the position in which they were before, for one of the very reasons that my hon. friend is trying to remedy this Bill of his, that is that they much prefer the decision of the Railway Commission that enables them to do away with the granting of any privilege to any particular class of shipper or class of people, While at this moment the rates on western grain may not appear so very burdensome simply because the grain is double the price it was a year ago, yet the grain was practically all out of the hands of the farmers before the rise in price came about.
Things had reached such a point a year ago that there was no profit or mighty little, for the farmer who produced the grain. The cost of taking a bushel of wheat from Winnipeg to Liverpool was from 6 to 8 cents higher than for two years previously. This was all brought about by mergers and amalgamations among the lake and ocean transportation companies, and the farmer had to pay every cent of the increase. The Bill my hon. friend has introduced will remedy this to a very large extent. The steamship companies cannot suffer; for no one can make me believe that the Railway Commission is not absolstely fair, or that it will deal unfairly with railroads, steamship companies or the public. We can safely leave the matter to them. I trust the Minister of Railways will accept this Bill and see that it becomes law this session.

maintopic: FIRST CANADIAN CONTINGENT- SUPPLY OF CARTRIDGES.
speechtext:
I desire to make a few remarks in regard to this Bill, and to say at the outset that I approve of the principle of bringing navigation companies on the lakes, and their tolls, under the control of the Railway Commission just as railway rates are under its control.	I have not been able to
gather from my hon. friend's remarks the relative charges of the railroads, the lake and the steamship companies. Personally I do not know exactly how much the lake companies charge for carrying a bushel of wheat from Fort William to Montreal, for instance, or how much the ocean companies charge for carrying it

from Montreal to Liverpool. If we had that information we should be in a better position to know exactly- where the high rates come in. In western Canada we have been inclined to blame the railroads more than the steamship companies, and we have had the idea that ocean rates are perhaps higher than they should be; but as a rule, I have not heard much criticism in western Canada of the companies operating on the Great Lakes. My hon. friend spoke about competition, and would have us believe that there is no competition on the Great Lakes; but I have always understood, although I may be wrong, that there was competition between American companies and American ports and Canadian companies and Canadian ports. It is a matter of great importance that our tolls on the Great Lakes should not be too high, and I am sure that if the navigation companies are put under the Railway Commission they will be fairly dealt with. If the companies are not charging too much I cannot see why they should not at once agree to come under the commission, but if they are charging too much I can see why they would be afraid to come under its jurisdiction. It would be a most fortunate thing for the people of Canada to know that they were being charged fair rates by the navigation companies. It has always seemed to me that any great corporation using the public utilities whether canals, lakes, or the right of way, should be under the control of the Parliament of Canada through a commission of some sort. That is only due to the people of this country, who are paying for these great public utilities. It is important that our rates on the lakes should be low, not only for the purpose of building up our Great Lake ports but, as my hon. friend from Lambton has said, for the benefit of all the producers in this country. For these reasons I think every member in this House might well give his support to this Bill.

maintopic: FIRST CANADIAN CONTINGENT- SUPPLY OF CARTRIDGES.
speechtext:
I was present before the committee, and had the opportunity of hearing some of the vesselmen who would be affected, presenting their views to the committee. I have also listened with some attention to the hon. gentleman who has just spoken, and to the hon. gentleman who has introduced this Bill. It seems only fair to the House, to the country, and to the enormous interests which would be affected, that I shoulu give, in the briefest possible fashion, the reason why the vesselmen believe it is not in the interests of the Canadian people that

this particular legislation should pass. And as I understand it manufacturers and shippers take practically this view. I have not the evidence before me, but I understand that is the case, and it is very easily explained.
Obviously the rates of the shipping companies on the Great Lakes have to be lower than railroad rates, because if they were not, the shipping companies would not get the business. They must beat the railroad rates, whether American or Canadian. Consequently, although the Railway Commission may fix reasonable railway rates in view of water and other competition, shipping companies have still to get under those rates. That is the first point. Secondly, the competition on the Great Lakes is not merely among Canadian shipping companies themselves but also with American shipping companies via Buffalo and New York. Consequently, to get grain from the head of the lakes to Montreal and thence to Liverpool, the rate on Canadian vessels has to be lower than on American vessels, or otherwise the grain would go via Duluth, Buffalo, and New York. Every one knows that the Buffalo and New York route, so far as the ocean end of it is concerned, has a great advantage over the Canadian route. New York is on what is called the Atlantic triangle. Vessels going from London to the Argentine come up the coast to New York, and then cross to London. The ocean rate is the one that very largely affects the situation, and over that rate, unfortunately, we have no control. From day to day and hour to hour during the grain season in this country, the competition is against New York and the New York route, and if by any chance the rates happen to be reasonably high, you can res.t assured that the Atlantic combine will take over all there is from Canada via New York; and we cannot touch them.

maintopic: FIRST CANADIAN CONTINGENT- SUPPLY OF CARTRIDGES.
speechtext: We do not permit that.

maintopic: FIRST CANADIAN CONTINGENT- SUPPLY OF CARTRIDGES.
speechtext:
This Bill does not touch them in any way. What the Canadian vessel owners say is: We want to get freight away from Buffalo and New York and into Canadian ships, Canadian channels, and Canadian ports. The only way to do that is from day to day and hour to hour to give a better rate, and we have done it this season. We have taken over ten millions of grain this season out of Chicago via Montreal, and it is the first time it has ever happened. If their view is correct,

how would iit be possible for the vessel owners of this country to give a better rate practically from day to day and hour to hour on grain, which is the most important product shipped out of this country, and on which every one wants to see the best possible rate given to the Canadian-farmer? We must make transportation as cheap as we can in this country. Farming is one of the most vital industries of Canada; more important than transportation, and unless we can give cheap rates the farming industry will not advance. The vessel people say: You will hinder us from doing the very thing you want to see brought about, because we have to be in a position to beat the Buffalo and New York route.
What has happened this year? Atlantic rates are higher to-day than they have ever been and the reasons for that are obvious. The rates on the Great Lakes have been lower than they have been for years We have had the spectacle of grain being carried from Port Arthur to Montreal for three and a half cents a bushel as against five, six and seven cents a bushel in other years. If there have been any combinations on the Great Lakes that have affected the matter they have affected it very beneficially for the Canadian farmer because if the Cana dian farmer had been getting anything like the same rates from the head of the lakes to the shipping point in the Canadian west or from Montreal to Liverpool he would have had a lower rate than that in force in any other country in the world.

maintopic: FIRST CANADIAN CONTINGENT- SUPPLY OF CARTRIDGES.
speechtext:
Is it not a fact that
more Canadian tonnage was under the jurisdiction of one company this year than in any other previous year?
' Mr. BRISTOL: Absolutely; there is no doubt about; it, but the result is that the company has been able to save nearly $300,000 in cost of operation and the Canadian farmer is getting his share of the benefit in a lower rate than has ever been known in this country before.

maintopic: FIRST CANADIAN CONTINGENT- SUPPLY OF CARTRIDGES.
speechtext: I would ask whether the American ships on the Great Lakes are under the control of the Inter-State Commerce Commission?

maintopic: FIRST CANADIAN CONTINGENT- SUPPLY OF CARTRIDGES.
speechtext:
I understand that those operated by railways are and that the others are not. But the boats we have to compete against in the grain trade are not operated by railways but by private shipping companies. Anybody can get into the shipping business. You can incorporate a
company; the Great Lakes are free to everybody and competition is absolutely keen. There is no opportunity to do anything different so long as Buffalo and New York are competing with Canadian shipping. We are deepening the Welland canal and I am sorry we are not also deepening the St. Lawrence. When you deepen the Welland canal what do the Americans do to meet that situation? They have paid many millions of dollars in building a canal from Oswego to the Erie canal so that when the Welland canal is deepened the big boats that now stop at Port Col-borne or Buffalo will go tc Oswego, Kingston or Prescott. The way the grain will go will depend precisely on what the rate is going to be between Oswego and New York. New York has a very great advantage over Montreal by reason of insurance rates, accessibility, and the tramp ships that come in there. One of the great troubles we have is the fact that on our northern route insurance on the vessels is greater and that the route itself is considered somewhat more dangerous than the New York route. The Canadian Government have been doing everything they possibly could do to make the St. Lawrence route as good as it can be made. I believe that we could canalize the St. Lawrence, and I believe that in doing it we would help the Canadian farmer, because the grain would go to Montreal and then be loaded into lighters or into ships going *abroad. That is the ideal shipping situation for this country to be in, and that is what we should aim at. I am satisfied that my hon. friend is introducing this Bill in absolute good faith, and I am satisfied that every hon .gentleman who supports it is supporting it in good faith, but 1 believe that we should pay heed to what the shipping interests say when they tell us that so long as they have to fight this American competition they cannot be giving a rate of tolls from hour to hour and minute to minute to the Railway Commission, that they have to be in a position from hour to hour in order to fight that competition, to give a better rate by Canadian boats and through Canadian channels, and that if you do not leave them in that position you are going to seriously hamper them in the competition that they have to meet in the shipping world to-day.

maintopic: FIRST CANADIAN CONTINGENT- SUPPLY OF CARTRIDGES.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had the honour last session to be a member of the joint committee, composed of members of

this House and of the Senate appointed to consider the consolidation of the Kailway Act, and this was one of the changes which it was intended to make and which was introduced by the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong). I am sorry that I did not hear that hon. gentleman throughout his speech. He presented his case very ably in the latter part of his speech, and, like my hon. friend from Centre Toronto (Mr. Bristol), I believe that the hon. gentleman who has introduced the Bill has done so with the very best of intentions, and I also believe there are many people who think that the adoption of this Bill would be of very great benefit to the Canadian people. I do not think I can present the evidence that was taken before that committee last year in any better manner than it has been presented by the hon. member for Centre Toronto. The great question that was raised there by the shippers who opposed this amendment was, just as he has stated, that the task which the steamboat owners had to perform was to successfully meet competition from their American rivals and they represented, as I understood their story, that in the United States the 'steamboats and vessels which were directly connected with the railways were under the jurisdiction of the Inter-State Commerce Commission. This is a grave situation. If the situation on the Great Lakes is as grave as it was represented to be by those who opposed this amendment last year, I think we should come to a decisibn in regard to this Bill only after the most mature consideration. My hon. friend who introduced the Bill tells us -that because steamships are connected with railway lines they are under the jurisdiction of the Railway Board and he argues that therefore all ships should be under the jurisdiction of the same board. I do not follow him in that contention. There are very good and very serious reasons why ships connected with railways should be under the jurisdiction of the Railway Board, which I suppose is responsible to Parliament. I do not know whether it is responsible to Parliament or not, but I suppose that if it does not do right the Government can dismiss it. There is not a railway in the Dominion but has received aid from the Government, and the Government must necessarily be interested in the proper conduct of these railways because the country's money has been invested in them. I suppose that is true of every railway built in Canada since Con-
federation. When these railways operate boats there is good reason why this Government should have some say in preventing these boats from putting on exorbitant rates. The Government exercises that control through the instrumentality of the Railway Board. But the question that we are now considering is an entirely different one. When it is proposed to place under the jurisdiction of the Railway Board vessels under private ownership which have never received anything from the Government by way of subvention or anything else, the proposal is one involving a very important departure from the policy which has hitherto been pursued. I do not pretend to be a very great constitutional lawyer but I have serious doubts as to whether or not the Railway Department, leaving the Railway Board out of the question, could take control of the shipping interests. The Railway Department has a man of good business capacity -at its head at the present, but if he should propose to take control of the shipping interests a considerable howl would go up and I believe the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries _ (Mr. Hazen) would say: Hands off; you may be well able to look after the railway interests but I have been appointed to look after the marine interests.
What difference is there between the Minister of Railways taking control of the shipping interests of this country and a board or commission appointed by him doing so? That is a question that should be submitted to the Minister of Justice for his consideration. Doubtless my hon. friend who has introduced this Bill has some very good reason for introducing it in this form; but, while there may be some excuse for bringing common carriers under the jurisdiction of the Railway Board, ships owned and controlled by people who ship only their own products in their own ships should not come under this Bill, and ships chartered by the season by companies or individuals who ship in such ships only their own products, should not come under this Bill. I have in mind several companies in the lower provinces, namely, the Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company, the Dominion Coal Company and the Dominion Steel Company, all of which absolutely control their own ships. The Dominion Steel Company has a magnificent fleet of ships plying between Sydney and Montreal, and also with Newfoundland. The Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company have also a very large fleet of ships plying to and from Montreal, Sydney, New Glasgow, and in fact every place where they can sell a bar of

steel or a pound of coal. Their ships carry nothing but the products of the mines of their owners or the products of the steel works; they are in no sense common carriers, and I do not think it would be fair to place them in the same position as common carriers. Owing to the very strong evidence which I heard given before the committee last year by the shipping interests of this country, and owing to the fact that they would be unduly hampered in their competition with the United States, I object to the passage of this Bill. I have not heard their objection answered. If it is answered to my satisfaction, then, of course, my objection to that phase of the Bill will fall to the ground.
As I pointed out a moment ago, I think the Minister of Justice should take the matter into consideration and give his legal opinion as to whether or not the Department of Railways or the Railway Commission can take control. Is it not the function of the Minister of Marine to institute a board to look after this matter?

maintopic: FIRST CANADIAN CONTINGENT- SUPPLY OF CARTRIDGES.
speechtext: The Minister of Railways is also the Minister of Canals, and as such has jurisdiction over the public canals. On that ground alone he can take control over the rates of the railways that use the public canals.

maintopic: FIRST CANADIAN CONTINGENT- SUPPLY OF CARTRIDGES.
speechtext: That is a very small part of my objection. Canadian ships coming to and from Canada pass through other waters than our canals.

maintopic: FIRST CANADIAN CONTINGENT- SUPPLY OF CARTRIDGES.
speechtext: The St. Lawrence channels, for instance, made by the Government.

maintopic: FIRST CANADIAN CONTINGENT- SUPPLY OF CARTRIDGES.
speechtext: I do not think the Minister of Railways contends that his department has any exclusive jurisdiction over the river St. Lawrence or the gulf of St. Lawrence or the waters into which the river St. Lawrence flows. As a Nova Scotian, I am not so very much interested in the traffic on the Great Lakes, but as a Canadian I am deeply interested. My chief objection to the Bill is that if it passes it will embrace common carriers. I contend that it should not embrace a line of steamships exclusively engaged in carrying the produce of one company from the place of production to its destination.

maintopic: FIRST CANADIAN CONTINGENT- SUPPLY OF CARTRIDGES.
speechtext:
I have listened with a good deal of interest to the remarks of my hon. friend the member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong), and I believe he is perfectly sincere in his desire to have this Bill pass. Having been, however, in the steamboat business for a number of years, but fortunately now 17
being out of it, I can see that if this Bill is passed, it will cause all sorts of complications. If the hon. member for East Lamb-ton was thoroughly familiar with the port of Montreal, for example, and the thousands of small ships owned by different individuals that trade between the port of Montreal and the ports of the lower St. Lawrence in the different parts of Quebec, he would see it would be almost impossible to put such boats under the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission. If we attempted to do that, we would put the small boat owners absolutely out of business. A great many of the men owning boats that operate on the lower St. Lawrence are uneducated, not being able to read or write, and they have trouble enough now endeavouring to make a small living out of the operation of their boats, because of the slowness of time in the carrying of freight between ports and the giving to the people of a service probably once every week or once every two weeks, as the case may be.
The manner in which freight rates are arrived at with regard to package freight for carriage on the Great Lakes is that the steamboat owners take the freight and work on a differential basis. The differential between Montreal and Port Arthur, for example, runs from two cents for fifth-class freight to either eight or ten cents for first-class freight. Let us suppose that I am operating a line of steamers from Montreal to Port Arthur to connect with the railroads there, and that I am running a boat a day and giving quicker service from Montreal to Winnipeg than do the railroads, is there any reason why I should not be allowed to charge the shippers, as much money as the railroads do? I cannot see any reason why I should not, and I am satisfied that the Railway Commission could not see any either. The Canadian steamship owners are giving a daily service out of Montreal and are operating at a less cost than the railways, on a first-class rate of ten cents per 100 lb., and a fifth-class rate of two cents per hundred. The hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Bristol) has given reasons why the control of the grain carriers between Port Arthur and Liverpool via Montreal should be in the hands of the steamboat owners in order to enable them to meet competition via New York. If you attempt to put grain rates under the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission, you will practically ruin the Canadian shipping industry and drive all business via Buffalo and New York.
The same thing applies to the smaller boats in the province of Ontario. I live in a

COMMONfe
county in which the carriage of freight is practically dependent on the steamboat men. We have only one railroad there and only one line through the county. I know a number of men operating small boats on the Bay of Quinte and endeavouring to make a living. If you put them under the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission it will mean the introduction of men skilled in the formation of tariffs and so on, the elimination of the existing boat service, and bring about all kinds of trouble.

maintopic: FIRST CANADIAN CONTINGENT- SUPPLY OF CARTRIDGES.
FIRST CANADIAN CONTINGENT- SUPPLY OF CARTRIDGES.
speechtext: The middleman is getting it.

maintopic: FIRST CANADIAN CONTINGENT- SUPPLY OF CARTRIDGES.
speechtext:
If the farmer has the wheat, he is getting the price. I do not know that it is much of an argument as suggested by my hon. friend (Mr. Bradbury) to say that the wheat is out of the hands of the farmer. There is a good deal of wheat still in the farmers' hands, and most of what has been sold did not get out of their hands until a very good price was received. If we could have a guarantee that in the future the farmer should not find it necessary to let the wheat out of his hands for a lower price than that which he is receiving this year, I do not know that we should object to paying a good, round freight rate, whether by land or water. But we can only judge the future by the past, and, judging in that way, we must conclude that the conditions which have existed will return. During the last four or five years, and until war conditions prevailed, it did not pay the farmer to raise wheat. Now, from the time the farmer begins to prepare his land for the crop until the grain reaches the market, it is the duty of this Parliament, in the interests of the whole people, whether in the East or in the West, to give us the most favourable conditions. What shall we say about the Railway Commission? My opinion is that commissions may come and commissions may go, but the Railway Commission will go on for ever. Why? Because never in the history of this country has any commission given such general satisfaction. Some hon. mdmber said that he did not know that the railways would be very anxious to have the Railway Commission discontinue. I do not agree with him. The railways of this country are not very fond of the present Railway Commission. This commission has been fair, and because of its great popularity the railways have not seen fit-and rightly too-to take the unpopular side and oppose the commission. I believe that we in western Canada have much to thank the Railway Commission for. Of course, the Railway Commission does not operate in exactly the same way as it did when it was inaugurated. How do we know but that from a small beginning-and I do not mean anything offensive to the promoter of the Bill in that-we may develop another body which will be as useful as the Railway Commission? Let us start somewhere. If we have been so successful in relieving the western farmer through the Railway Commission, we have a right to believe that we shall be just as successful with a commission controlling the rates by water.

The only objection I have to this Bill is that it does not go far enough. It controls rates, as I understand, only on inland waters. It is stated by some hon. gentleman on the other side that the Bill should not apply to private companies, but that we have a perfect right to apply it to companies that receive subsidies from this Parliament. But, even though we are not granting subsidies in actual money to these companies, we have spent, are spending, and will spend in the future, immense sums of money in aids to navigation, in docks, harbours and canals, for the development of this business. Hence, I cannot see why these companies should be exempt from [DOT] control. The new commission, should one be appointed and charged with this duty of regulation, may be counted upon to be as fair to all companies as the Railway Commission has been to the railway companies. We must realize that wheat is not always going to be $1.50 a bushel-if it were I might not be supporting my hon. friend's Bill. But, in view of the change that may be expected to take place in the market conditions, the real business of this Parliament is to do its utmost to enable the farmers of Canada to send their products to the market at the lowest possible cost.

maintopic: FIRST CANADIAN CONTINGENT- SUPPLY OF CARTRIDGES.
speechtext:
The riding which I have the honour to represent is very much interested in the growth and development of large grain ports, especially in view of the fact that the Canadian Pacific railway have elevators at Port McNicoll, and the Grand Trunk railway elevators at Midland. The fact that the business of transportation of grain through Canada has not increased as we hoped it would is my reason for rising to give my opinion of this proposed legislation.
While some gentlemen who have supported the Bill have made many statements, I regret that few of them have been statements of fact. One would almost imagine that the freight rates on the Great Lakes have been going up by leaps and bounds for the last ten years. Perhaps it will surprise hon. gentlemen when I tell them that there was a time when the freight rate from Fort William to Midland was seven cents a bushel, and that last year it was about one cent a bushel. I have in my hand the report of the Chamber of Commerce of Buffalo-the rates to Georgian bay ports are about on a parity with the rates to Buffalo-and for the benefit of hon. gentlemen and for future reference I will quote the rates in force previous to 1908.
In 1897, the range of rates on wheat from Duluth to Buffalo was 1-24 cents; 1898, 1-34 cents; 1899, 24-6 cents; 1900, 14-3J cents; 1901, 14-3| cents; 1902, 1-24 cents; 1903, 14-2| cents; 1904, 1-5 cents; 1905, 14-4 cents; 1906, lf-3 cents; 1907, 1-24 cents; 1907, 1-24 cents; 1908, 1-34 cents.
There is no report later than that for the year 1908, but I can say that so low were-the rates last year that a large number of vessels were tied up, on the American as well as on the Canadian side; the rates would not pay investors to go into the business. When the Algonquin first went on the lakes twenty or twenty-five years ago, the rate in the fall was seven cents a bushel, the reason being that there were very few vessels then in the grain business. I wonder if hon. gentlemen know how trade has grown particularly in respect of American vessels.
I ho id in my hand a book commonly known as the Great Lakes Red Book, issued in 1912. It gives the name of one vessel, the William P. Snider, with a tonnage of 13,000 tons, and scores of others with tonnages of
8.000,	10,000, and so on. As a rule the Can- . adian vessels are small, having a tonnage of about 3,500 tons. What is the real position of this grain trade? It is admitted that in the United States there are no restrictions in the shape of commissions hampering or interfering with the vessel owner or with the grain owner. It should be remembered, after all, that the grain owner, is the man who dictates the route which the grain will take. If the grain owner has a million bushels of grain in the Port Arthur elevators, it is to him not a matter of sentiment, but a matter of business whether he ships it by Buffalo or by Montreal. My hon. friend the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Bristol) made the statement, which everybody knows is correct, that the rates from New York are always lower than those from Montreal. Some hon. gentleman referred to the fact in i>- there was an abnormal output from M a',real last year. I have sent for one of .a ceports, and I find that during the yea 1913-19K 70,000,000 bushels of wheat we

 sent out of Montreal, and during the year before, 41.000.000. In 1897 the amount of wheat sent out was
11.000.	000 bushels. Living at Midland, I know that prior to the war it was a matter of common knowledge that through that port there was passing a lot of wheat for Germany last year, and that the increase of 30,000,000 bushels at Montreal was due to to the fact that the German Government or German dealers in grain, in view of the impending war, were buying largely, and

were having the grain shipped via Montreal. I presume that was the reason for the vast increase of 30,000,000 bushels.
What are we going to do if we pass legislation like this? A man who owns grain in the Northwest will ship it by the Soo line to Duluth; it will then go on American vessels to Buffalo and be transhipped to England or other European country. It will not be interfered with by any commission in Canada, because no commission will deal with it in the United States. On the other hand, supposing a grain dealer should wish to send shipments by Fort William or via the Canadian Northern to Port Arthur; he is not bound to be under the ban of the Railway Commission, because it will be no contravention of the coasting laws to employ American vessels to take that grain from Port Arthur to Buffalo. It is in the fall of the year, when grain is passing out rapidly, that the Canadian vessel owner is looking for freights. In this little red book there is arranged a list of what are known as ore carriers, of which, I think, there are about 600.	Some	of these are of
Canadian register and some American. Any vessel which is of such strength that you can shoot ore into its hold will easily carry grain, but any vessel that will carry grain will not necessarily be strong enough to carry a cargo of ore. Hon. gentlemen who have seeit ore rushing into the bottom of a vessel realize that for that particular purpose a vessel of superior strength is needed. I take it, therefore, that there are not only upwards of 600 ore vessels in the trade, but two or three thousand large grain vessels in Canada and the United States. What are you going to do about it? Last year Canadian trade was in an apathetic state and competition with American carriers was so keen that Canadian vessels by the score were tied up. Vessels were tied up in Midland which in other years were probably getting two or three cents a bushel for carrying grain. The same conditions prevailed at the Soo, in the Detroit river and elsewhere. The ship lines of Canada made no money last year. The largest of them, the Canada Steamship line, passed its dividend; many others did the same, and some of them paid a very much decreased dividend. The passing of legislation of this kind means that the grain owner, who, I repeat, does not consider sentiment in the matter, may take his grain to Duluth by the Canadian Pacific railway and via American lines. The American system owned by the Hill people fMr. W. H. Bennett.]
crosses into Manitoba and from the Northwest ; and grain may by this line be brought down to Duluth, and the grain owner will not be hampered by the control of freight rates by a commission. In that respect you take the chance of hitting your Canadian railways. Of course, the Canadian Pacific railway can bring the grain to Duluth on their own line just as conveniently as they can bring it to Fort William, but it is the vesselman who will be hit, and hit the hardest-the vessel man who in Canada to-day is not getting within two or three cents a bushel of the rates that he got a few years ago. Despite the vast .export from Montreal, last year such a state of things existed that the owners were compelled in many instances to tie up their vessels. These men will be in this position, that the ore trade being over in the United States, immense carriers like the Snider, with a capacity of 13,000 tons or 450,000 to 500,000 bushels of wheat, having made a good season in the ore business, will take on board cargoes from Port Arthur or Fort William for Buffalo at seven-eighths of a cent per bushel, as was the case last year; whereas the Canadian vessel, which cannot enter the ore trade owing to the American coasting laws, must wait for the Canadian wheat trade in the fall, and then cannot meet such a price as that charged by these immense carriers, the capacity of the Canadian vessels being usually about 100,000 bushels. This competition tends to divert the wheat from the Canadian Georgian bay ports or St. Law'rence ports to American ports. Not only are the two ports in my constituency deeply concerned in this, but also Goderich, Collingwood and the other ports on our lower lakes. The menwho are endeavouring to build up a vessel trade in Canada are seriously handicapped in this way. It may be said, of course, that they are permitted to engage in the coal carrying trade from American ports to Fort William and Port Arthur in the summer, but there they have the competition of old American sailing vessels which are now used as tow barges and which, owing to their age and inferiority, carry the coal at rates which would be quite impossible for the Canadian steamships as the Canadian vessels, in order to comply with the insurance requirements for the carrying of grain, must be of a very much better class. It must be remembered that the proportion of American shipping to Canadian shipping is about seventy to one. The moment you place the Railway Commission over vessels this result will come about that the owner of the grain will be fearful that rates may

be imposed which are not now imposed by reason of the keen competition on the lakes to-day and the grain would be diverted to Buffalo and other American ports by these vessels. It would be an unfortunate thing for the Canadian vessel owner and for Canadian ports. The records show that the rates to Buffalo and to Georgian bay ports are the same. The freight rates on the Great Lakes are not high. They are decreasing and have decreased abnormally, and in view of the fact that while on the other side enterprise and capital have gone into the business of placing ships on the Great Lakes so that their merchant marine is firmly established, there are
5 p.m. comparatively few Canadian-owned vessels. These vessels should be given a fair chance and we should not pass legislation that can have but one effect, that of causing the shipper of grain to prefer the American ships and American avenues of trade rather than Canadian ships and Canadian avenues of trade.

maintopic: FIRST CANADIAN CONTINGENT- SUPPLY OF CARTRIDGES.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have undertaken to deal in Parliament with the general transportation question. We have regulated the railways and we propose now to regulate the inland steamboats, and if I had my way we would regulate the ocean rates as weli. I believe that ocean rates can easily be brought within the jurisdiction of this Parliament and it would be absurd for this country to continue spending the millions we are spending on the solution of the transportation problem unless we deal with the question as a whole, embracing railroads, inland navigation and ocean freight rates. One great principle that must be kept in mind is that water transportation and land transportation ought to be complementary one of the other. That has been worked out in Germany and in other countries and if a freight company can use both railroad and water transportation it should be compelled to do so. The question is not, as it was put by the hon. member for Centre Toronto, whether the steamships charge less than the railways, but do they _ charge a rate that gives a fair margin above the actual cost? So the man or the state that proposes to deal with transportation must deal with land transportation and with water transportation-and by water transportation I mean both on inland waters and on the high seas. So it is well within the jurisdiction of this House to deal with this question, and it is the duty of this House in dealing with transportation to regulate the rates on water as well as on land. It will be idle for us to spend any money in improving our inland navigation if we do not get the benefit of that improvement, because the more canals we build and the cheaper we make transportation, unless we regulate the steamboat lines, the more they will benefit by the reduction in cost of operation. If these things are true we ought to take control of the boats as well as of the railroads, and if we do take control we will not try to prevent the boat lines giving the claimed low service they have been giving to our people, but will prevent them doing any injustice. Inland transportation rates have often been the same as railway rates. They should not be as high as railway rates and we should have been able to prevent such a charge. We are told that we will be asked some day to allow a great railway company in this country to segregate its assets and take its boats and its steamship lines out of the control of the main company and put them under a company that would be purely a navigation or sea-going steamship company. If we had not control over the inland transportation of a railway, we might in this case lose control of it altogether. If we have control of a railway we ought also to have control of the boats, and it is only in that way that we can regulate transportation and get lower rates. Furthermore, if the proposal which the hon. gentleman has introduced to-day was in the Government measure of last session, why is not the Railway Act to he dealt with this session? We, ought to have the Railway Bill before the House to-day, because the dislocation that has come to this country by reason of the war calls for regulation of the great corporations that seek to give public service to this country, whether banks, railway companies, irland transportation companies or ships upon the sea. We ought to be dealing with this transportation question in a broad way, and I hope the Minister of Railways will announce to-day that he is going on with this measure, so that it will not be necessary for private members to bring in Bills that seek to put in force some of the good principles that were incorporated in the Government Bill of last session. It would be to the great benefit of this country if we dealt with the transportation question this session, and put in force not only the clause which the hon. gentleman has introduced to-day but nearly all the clauses in the estimable Government Bill of last session. We should then be trying to get good
26:

rates. As the hon. member (Mr. Schaffner) has just said, it is not of so much importance to the farmers this year because the price of grain is high; but we do not know how long that high price will continue. And I absolutely endorse what he has said and what the commission in the West found out that grain-growing is almost impossible in this country at the price obtained by farmers in the last few years. Furthermore, as grain went down in price, freignt rates went up. In fact the whole tendency for the past few years has been to reduce the price that the farmer obtains for his wheat and to increase the cost of carriage. We shall not be able to populate the West and make it a successful farming country unless we control the rates charged on the produce of that country. We may subsidize railways, build competing lines, spend our money as freely as we like, but unless we adopt regulation of transportation as a principle, and in that direction, we shall be throwing our money away and not be helping to settle the West. The problem to-day is to settle the Canadian West and to restore prosperity to that country. Instead of only two per cent of the agricultural lands being occupied they should all be occupied. But to do that we must be able to say: We are going to give you a fair deal, you shall get a fair share of the product of your labour. Apparently there is no way of doing that and of holding out the lamp of hope to attract settlers to the West, except by regulation of transportation. When you adopt a great principle of that kind there is bound to be injustice in various directions. All practical legislation does more or less injustice; but it works. This principle could be applied and public relief attained, but only by making the principle broad and giving it a fair interpretation ; and you can trust any public commission such as the Railway Board, to do justice, to secure fair treatment to the companies who give the service, and to injure nobody. I heard apologies made in this House to-day for a great transportation company that only a year ago was authorized to do what it liked in connection with its capitalization. That company has not been successful in making money on the enormous flotation it put out some months ago. But that is largely the fault of this Parliament. We should have kept control of the capitalization of that company, and if we had that control and control of its rates, we should be in a better position to-day to compel them to do what this Bill seeks to do: to treat the public fairly, to give a good 
service; and those who give the service should get a fair remuneration for it, based on its actual cost. I should lik* to see the House seized of this Bill, and the Bill of last session We should prepare now to take up the new duty that comes to Canada by reason of the dislocation the war has caused, and we should approach these new conditions with transportation under the control of Parliament by way of a commission, whether transportation by lake, rail, river or canal.

speechtext: Just a few words in answer to the objections made by different members. The hon. member for South York and the hon. member for Souris are supporting the measure. They merely ask that we shall have control of ocean freight rates as well.

speakeroldname: Hon. F. COCHRANE (Minister of Railways and Canals):
maintopic: FIRST CANADIAN CONTINGENT- SUPPLY OF CARTRIDGES.

maintopic: FIRST CANADIAN CONTINGENT- SUPPLY OF CARTRIDGES.
speechtext: The question of the second reading is not disposed of yet, and consequently the hon. gentleman cannot make his motion now. They cannot do so after he has spoken.

maintopic: FIRST CANADIAN CONTINGENT- SUPPLY OF CARTRIDGES.
speechtext:
I wish to thank the Minister of Railways for being good enough to let this Bill go to the committee.
I am satisfied that when the evidence on both sides is heard the committee will unanimously decide in favour of the Bill. The hon. member for South York and the hon. member for Souris have called attention to ocean * freight rates and urged that the Bill should give us control over those rates. That is quite impossible here. These gentlemen know that a commission has been appointed by this Government for the purpose of investigating freight rates on the ocean, and that commission is acting jointly with a similar commission appointed

by the British Government and have this matter under consideration. There is a provision in this Bill which requires that ocean vessels coming to our ports shall file their tolls and tariff arrangements and agreements at those ports. I am satisfied if that should become established the commission that is appointed to investigate ocean freight rates will be materially assisted. The hon. member for East Simcoe called attention to the fact that the United States has not any legislation similar to this applicable to shipping having coasting privileges along the shores of the United States. That is true; but at the present time Congress has under consideration a Bill which proposes to control such rates and to place them under a commission in the United States. They have had during the past two years a commission investigating this question and have decided to bring in a Bill, not similar to this, but one whereby they will be able to place vessels in their inland waters under the control of a commission.
The hon. member for East Simcoe quoted a number of rates in force to-day, but you will quite understand that these are the lowest rates that are given to the port of Midland. He also called attention to the fact that we are at the mercy of the vesselmen of the United States. The increased export through Montreal goes to show the enormous extension of the trade of that port and the need of such legislation as I am proposing. The volume of the transportation of grain through our ports is constantly increasing.
The hon. member for Central Toronto (Mr. Bristol) called attention to the fact that some of the manufacturers in eastern Canada are opposed to this legislation. 1 am quite aware of that. Large manufacturers, who to-day are receiving special privileges, or the lowest possible rates, from the vessel-men on inland waters-and I am not objecting to these reasonably low rates because they have tremendous quantities of goods to be carried by these vessels-are the only manufacturers who are coming forward to object to this measure. On the other hand, practically all the smaller manufacturers and shippers will welcome this measure in order that they may be able to have the rates applied in such a manner as the Board of Railway Commissioners will apply them. We have a statement from one hon. gentleman in opposition to this Bill to the effect that the freight rates on the inland waters should not exceed those
on the railways, or that they should compare favourably with them. What an absurd statement to make, because when you take into consideration the fact that there are boats on the inland waters that are capable of carrying 250,000 or 300,000 bushels of grain, and that these boats can be operated at a cost of $250 per day, you can readily understand the small amount of actual cost involved in the transportation of these products from western ports to the port of Montreal.
I do not know that there were any other statements made seriously objecting to this measure. The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Carroll) gave his assurance that he would not oppose this Bill if people who own private steamboats or vessels are not interfered with, such as the Steel Company. I might call his attention to the fact that this Bill will have no effect on companies, such as the Steel Company, who own, control and operate their own boats. Therefore, I will in the future look for his sympathy in connection with this measure. I again wish to thank my hon. friend the Minister of Railways for agreeing to refer this measure to the Railway Committee, and I feel confident that we will be able to establish justification for taking the action we have.
