speechtext: On the order for resuming the adjourned debate on the proposed motion of Mr. Bick-erdike for the second reading of Bill No. 18, to amend the Criminal Code:

speakeroldname: Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) :
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: FIRST CANADIAN CONTINGENT- SUPPLY OF CARTRIDGES.
speechtext:
I had not the pleasure or the advantage of being present when the motion of my hon. friend from Montreal, (Mr. Bickerdike) for the second reading of the measure which he proposes, was moved. I have, however, taken occasion to read carefully the report of what was said by 'my hon. friend and by other hon. members who took part in the discussion on this very important question. It is unnecessary for me to say that my hon. friend who is my neighbour in the city of Montreal, put his motion before the House, in such a manner as to win our sympathy for the cause he is advocating. No one questions the absolute sincerity of the view that he puts forward on this very important question, nor would any one be disposed to question that he supported that view with arguments that are worthy of the most careful consideration. Neither do I think that there is any need of saying anything about the importance of the question itself. It is one that has for a long period of time engaged the attention of, I think I can without exaggeration say, the civilized peoples of the world. It is one too upon which there has been a very marked divergence of opinion. I am "certainly free to concede that upon the side of this question which the hon. member (Mr. Bickerdike) has taken up there can be invoked the authority of names entitled to the very highest respect, as well as arguments of the very greatest weight.
In the United Kingdom in 1864, a committee was appointed to consider this matter and upon that committee were men of the very highest standing in the legal, profession and in the public life of the country. The result of the deliberations of that committee was that its-members were practically equally divided upon the question whether or not capital punishment should be abolished. That means that upon both sides of the question one could invoke the authority of the most eminent and most qualified men to judge, to.be found in the United Kingdom at that time. That fact alone demonstrates that we are dealing with a question upon which no one can undertake to speak dogmatically, or which can be looked upon as one having anything even approaching but one side to it.
[Mr. Cochrane.!
I do not purpose going seriatim into the arguments advanced in support of this Bill. I may say at once that they have not carried to me the conviction that, at the present time at all events, this measure should pass into law. The basic argument-if I correctly grasp the effect of what the hon. member who introduced this Bill said- upon which he founds his contention, is that there is no right in the State to take any man's life. I understand him to take the most absolute view of the effect of the prohibition, " Thou shalt not kill ". In the first place, before I touch the question whether there is any distinction to be made between the individual and the authority vested by society in the head of the State, when you come to the application of that prohibition, I think it may be well to point out what is obvious to us all, that even as regards that prohibition a$ addressed to the individual, it is not possible to accept it as being as absolute as the hon. member would seem to consider it. For instance, I do not think it would be suggested even by the hon. member himself that the individual is so absolutely bound by that prohibition that under no circumstances whatsoever would he be justified in killing a human being. Take for instance, a case that presents itself at the very first glance to every one-the case of self-defence. Surely no one would suggest that the prohibition is so absolute that when some man, armed to take my life, attacks me, I must, to conform with the reasonable requirement of the prohibition, stand quietly and allow him to kill me. It must be present to all our minds that there are other cases where the prohibition is not of absolute application. On the battlefields of Europe to-day our brothers, those of our own blood, those of our own immediate country, are engaged in the destruction of human life. We are making great sacrifices to fit them out and equip them so that they may be able to act with the greatest effect in that work in which they are engaged. I am satisfied that my patriotic friend from St. Lawrence will not suggest that those men are violating the command for which he, in common with us all, has such a very great respect. Therefore in so far as the contention is that the prohibition is so absolute that neither the State nor the individual can have any right under any circumstances to violate its letter, I need not spend more time in meeting it.
It seems to me also that there is a distinction to be made between the effect of that prohibition as addressed to the indi-

vidual and its effect when you seek to apply it to the governing power of the State, which is charged with the defence and the preservation of the State, just as the individual is charged with his own defence and his own preservation. And if it be true that the individual, when it is necessary for the preservation of his own life, is entitled to treat the prohibition a? not applicable, I hardly think it can be claimed that, where the State, responsible for the protection of society and of all its members, finds it necessary in discharge of that paramount duty to take human life, it can be held to have violated that prohibition.
It seems to be contended that there is some more absolute right to life on the part of the individual than there is to any other possession of his, and more especially it is manifestly the contention of the supporters of this Bill that the individual has a more absolute right to his life than he has to his liberty, because what is proposed is not that we should let the guilty man, who to-day is condemned to lose his. life, go free; what is proposed is that we should deprive him of his liberty. I think that on reflection it will appear clear that man's right to his life is no more absolute than his right to his liberty. It may be that in one ease the object of the right is more precious or more valuable than in the other; but that does not alter the nature of the right, though it may affect the interest which a man has in asserting its inviolability. Whether life is more precious than liberty is a question on which there may very well be a difference of opinion. Certainly, the people who have at all times been most highly admired and commended are those who thought that liberty was more precious than life.

maintopic: FIRST CANADIAN CONTINGENT- SUPPLY OF CARTRIDGES.
speechtext:
I would remind the hon. minister of that great Irishman who said, " Give me liberty or give me death."
Mr. W. F. MACLEAN; No, he was a Scotch-American. His name wag Patrick Henry, but Patrick is an Aberdeen name.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: FIRST CANADIAN CONTINGENT- SUPPLY OF CARTRIDGES.
speechtext: If he was not an Irishman, he had the best of names, and when a man has the best of names, I can excuse the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) for thinking that he must be an Irishman.

maintopic: FIRST CANADIAN CONTINGENT- SUPPLY OF CARTRIDGES.
speechtext: He deserved to be.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: FIRST CANADIAN CONTINGENT- SUPPLY OF CARTRIDGES.
speechtext:
Patrick Henry, whatever may have been his nationality, was among those who expressed the view that liberty is more precious than life. That is a view with which one may concur in without fear, at all events, of finding himself otherwise than in the very best of company.
I am entirely unable to see what distinction can be made between the right to life and the right to liberty. If the proposition upon which this measure is based be that the right to life is so absolute that under no circumstances has the State the right to deprive a man of it, then it seems clear to me that it should apply equally to the right to liberty. Or, if it be alleged that the object of the right to life is more precious than the object of the right to liberty, I cannot see that reason has been given for making such a distinction. Looking at the matter from the point of view of abstract principle simply, I therefore find it impossible to follow the hon. member.
Now, if we could conceive of circumstances in which an individual, even when he becomes a member of society, retains rights so absolute that it is not to give way in the face of the superior right of the State to do the things essential for its preservation and for the effective carrying out of the duties incumbent upon those who are charged with the authority of the State, then I presume that a man's right to his life might be counted as among those absolute rights. But we must remember that, whatever may be the absolute right of the individual when he stands alone, yet, when he forms one unit in a great society his right must yield in order that the society of which he is a member may properly perform its functions and may secure to him, in common with all his fellow-members of that society, these very advantages, the assurance of which to the indiviuual is the purpose for which society exists.
If I am right in this, all we have to ask ourselves is; Is the continuance of capital punishment necessary as a means for the repression of crime? For my part, I am willing to go further and to ask: Is it uesirable for the enabling of society or tne State to perform its duty of securing to those who are in its charge in the enjoyment of their lives and their liberty? No man's right is so absolute that it must not yield in the face of the equal right of his neighbour, and no man's right is so absolute that it must not yield in the face of that which is necessary, or even desirable, to maintain that condition in which organized society may ensure to the individual the full measure of protection which it is the duty of the State to give, and the giving of which to its members is the one thing that justifies the

existence of the State and its rightful authority.
I know, it may be said, that it is upon those who advocate the maintenance of this form of punishment to demonstrate its necessity and desirability. The best answer to that is that those who maintain the rightfulness of this form of punishment are, in this country at all events, the parties in possession. They are able to invoke, moreover, the fact that from the earliest times down to a comparatively recent period, there has been common consent as to the right of the State to enforce this penalty, and as to its necessity and desirability. Some countries in modern times have done away with this penalty; all countries have reduced its application so that it comes into play only in respect of the very gravest crimes. In that regard I think we may all agree that they have acted wisely-and in saying that I do not think that we imply at all that it would be wiser for them to go further and apply it to crimes of all classes.
A great deal has been said in support of this measure as to the sacredness of human life. I think the very sacredness of human life is the strongest justification for the maintenance of this penalty. Human life is sacred; there is no doubt about that. The life of the criminal is, within the limits of the disposition of properly ordained law, sacred. But the lives of the innocent are sacred, too; the lives of the whole community-men, women and children-are just as sacred. Their enjoyment of life, free from apprehension, is a very sacred thing. We are apt to lose sight of that when we get face to face with one man who is going to be hanged. Advocates of this measure at once forget the other one man, or the other several men, perhaps, who stood facing the revolver of this condemned individual. One life is not more sacred than another. But, it will be said, by taking the one you will not revive the other; and that is perfectly true. But, I think we need nothing more to justify the maintenance of this penalty than that it operates to deter the commission of the crime for which it is inflicted. I do not conceive that it is incumbent upon us to show that it is necessary for the purposes of a deterrent. All we are called upon to show is that it. contributes to deterring, and adds an additional safeguard. Upon the question as to whether or not it operates as a deterrent, as upon all matters that touch this question, I am quite free to agree that there is anything but unanimity of opinion, and that people of the very highest authority have taken the view that the 
imposition of this penalty does not operate as a deterrent, or, at all events, not as a more effective deterrent than other means of punishment. When we are called upon to form an opinion about that, we are always asked to confine our attention to the individual man who has come to the stage of contemplating committing a murder aud it is said: , unless it can be established that the man at that moment stops and says to himself, veil, if it were not for the hanging that might follow, I would kill my neighbour, you have not shown any deterrent effect. I do not so understand at. The great deterrent effect, to my mind, .that the infliction of this penalty produces is the great deterrent effect upon the whole body of the community; upon the general mind; upon the manner in which the whole of the people look upon murder. It is in that respect that I think the argument fails, that because good efieets have followed upon the abolition of this penalty with regard to minor crimes, we should go further. I can quite understand that the deterrent effect of capital punishment was very much minimized when it was made of general application, so that any offence whatever which a man might be tempted to commit, or, at all events, offences even of a minor character which a man might be tempted to commit, exposed him to this ultimate penalty. Inasmuch as we cannot hope for a community exempt from temptation to crime or offence of any kind, that condition of affairs very naturally created the feeling which is expressed in the saying that one might as well be hanged for a sheep as for a lamb; if hanging is to be applicable to offences great and small, the effect is that you put all offences upon the same level. But when you single out this crime of murder, this crime of taking human life, and set it apart in a category with treason, which involves taking or attacking the life of the state itself; when you set it aside to have applied to it this extreme penalty, then, it seems to me, you infallibly set that 'crime apart as an uncommittable crime for the great bulk of the population. That, to me, is the deterrent effect that I argue for.
I am not prepared to argue, and I do not think it is necessary to argue, that when a man under the influence of passion, under the influence, perhaps,, of intoxicating drink or under the pressure of cupidity, has come to the point where he is willing to consider murder as among the possible things, he will stop because he

may be hanged. But I do contend-and this seems to me to be clear-.that the maintenance of this penalty is a great deterrent on the great mass- of the people. You keep this crime before them as the thing that may be compared to the scriptural unpardonable sin and the thing that the State visits with the last and ultimate penalty of deprivation of life. Doing that, you bring home	to	every	individual in the community just the extent to which	the State	appreciates the sacredness of human life. The state so appreciates that sacredness, it attaches such importance to enforcement of the prohibition: Thou shalt not kill, that before all its people it proclaims that towards the m^rti who takes his neighbour's life, the state has no disposition to exercise mercy or leniency. So, for my part, it is not a question at all of what the individual would-be murderer thinks at the moment that he is going to commit his crime; the great important matter is how the whole community will look upon the crime of slaying a human being. I think that we can make no mistake when we take the most extreme means that are at our disposal to create and maintain in the common mind of the whole people that absolute conviction that the man who kills another steps beyond the pale of compassion. '
So much for the deterrent effects of the maintenance of this form of punishment and if you once admit the deterrent effects I do not think I need spend time in arguing for the position: that the authority responsible for the protection of society and all its individual members, the authority to whom the individual owes allegiance purely and simply because it exists to give and does give him that protection, is bound to use effective means to secure it to him. I know that minor arguments are advanced. We are told of the terrible danger, in view of the fallibility of all human judgment of some innocent man being convicted and being executed. I think under our system of administration of justice, that while, of course, no one can say that that is not a possibility, at the very least we can safely claim that it is a most remote possibility; and if it should have to [DOT] be admitted that it might, after a long series of years, happen that one man, innocent of a crime, should unfortunately be convicted and executed, no doubt that would be a most lamentable thing. But for my part I would be quite prepared to set over against that the immense advantage which,
in my judgment at least, results to society at large and to every individual member of it from the maintenance of this most extreme form of punishment.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Bickerdike) spoke with a good deal of feeling of a case in which he said within the last year an innocent man had gone to the gallows. I happen to be familiar with that case. I am quite- sure that the hon. member will not find fault if I suggest that I had greater opportunity of knowing justwhat happened in that case than he could possibly have had. I have on my shoulders the responsibility of that man's life, jointly, of course, with my colleagues, but the initiative of the advice and the responsibility for it was mine; and might I say to the hon. gentleman that that man went to the gallows after a trial before a properly constituted court, before a jury of his countrymen who convicted him; and he went to the gallows after the perfect regularity and legality of the trial had been submitted to the Court of Appeals in his own province and then to the Supreme Court of Canada, and he went there under the unanimous judgment of that Supreme Court and under a disposition of law which, for my part, I would with great regret see disappear from the Criminal code of this country.

The House resumed at eight o'clock

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: FIRST CANADIAN CONTINGENT- SUPPLY OF CARTRIDGES.
speechtext:
When you
left the Chair, Mr. Speaker, I was proceeding to speak of a case which the non. member who introduced this Bill had referred to in his remarks as being a case where an innocent man had gone to the scaffold. In themselves the circumstances of that case are perfectly simple. I have no desire, it is not a pleasant task, to insist upon the guilt of one who has now gone before a higher and an infallible Judge. But the fact remains that, so far as it is possible for us with our limited capacity for judgment to reach a sound conclusion, I myself have no doubt that that man went to a deserved death. The innocent man for whom the hon. member's heart bleeds started out with another innocent man, each of them armed with revolvers loaded and prepared for action, on the laudable purpose of holding up whomsoever they might meet and robbing them at the point of the revolver. They intended to go in company with two others. Somehow or other their arrangement did not turn out as they expected. They missed the two

others, and from the innocent employment of holding up the passer-by they diverted tneir attention to the equally innocent employment of burglarizing a couple of stores. They achieved this laudable purpose, and proceeded to divide the swag. But while engaged in that perfectly innocent occupation a policeman was imprudent enough and inconsiderate enough to intrude upon them and the policeman was shot. Nobody knows till this hour which of those two men shot the policeman.

maintopic: FIRST CANADIAN CONTINGENT- SUPPLY OF CARTRIDGES.
speechtext:
Good!
Mr- DOHERTY:	But it is absolutely
certain that one of those two men shot the policeman. The hon. gentleman's interjection of " good " conveys his idea of immaculate innocence. In the eyes of the hon. member, the man that did not fire the shot is an innocent man. All that he did was to start out armed and equipped and ready for murder. All that he did was to go out with murder in his heart. All that he did was to prepare himself so that if somebody interfered with his robbery of his neighbours he would be in a position to murder that somebody. That is all. Perfect innocence! If you have tears, prepare to shed them now. This perfectly innocent gentleman-and I do not know which of these two was the perfectly innocent-gentleman, and nobody does-had only started out with that purpose. He had only started out with a companion inspired, to his knowledge, with the same purpose. The two of them had only gone out on an absolutely unlawful expedition in the course of which the two of them perfectly knew that murder was liable to be committed. They got ready for that. They went out, and what they perfectly knew might happen did happen. The barbarous representative of the law, the law that hangs men that murder their neighbours, ventured to interfere with them, and between the two of those men he was shot down and killed. There was not any possible doubt of all the facts that I have stated. These two men told us the story themselves. They agreed upon every incident until the moment of the firing of the shot; and then each said that the other man fired the shot. If we are to apply the doctrine that my hon. friend apparently thinks we should apply, then so far as we knew these were two absolutely innocent men who ought to have gone scot free.

maintopic: FIRST CANADIAN CONTINGENT- SUPPLY OF CARTRIDGES.
speechtext: I did not say so.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: FIRST CANADIAN CONTINGENT- SUPPLY OF CARTRIDGES.
speechtext:
It is absolutely certain that one of them fired the shot. The Parliament of this country has enacted that where 
two or more men prepare for the committing of a crime, join together in the attainment of an unlawful purpose in the pursuit of which it is probable that any crime may be committed, each one of them is responsible for whatever crime the other commits and that certainly was the case here. For my part, I would be sorry should that cease to be the law. There was an innocent policeman who went out in the performance of his duty to protect the lives and the property of the citizens of Vancouver, for it was in that city this happened. He lost ms life. My hon. friend does not seem to be impressed with the sacredness of his life; yet he was a perfectly innocent man. More than that, he was a brave man courageously doing his duty for the protection of the# citizens of this country, doing his duty in seeing that other people who slept quietly at home in their beds that night were protected from the nefarious operations of the man who has gone to the gallows, and that policeman was shot uown in cold blood without a moment's warning; was sent to his reckoning with his Creator without one instant of preparation. Human life is sacred, but my hon. friend has no sympathy to waste on the death of that man. His horror is that the two men were held responsible for'that crime, the two men who co-operated to bring about the conditions in which that policeman lost his life, the two men whom the law declared to be equally guilty whichever of them fired the shot and the actions of each of whom led up to and culminated in that crime. For my part, I have said it twice already, and I say it now, I hope the law in that respect may long remain on the statute book. I think it is an absolutely just, an absolutely equitable, an absolutely necessary law. I said that I was responsible for the advice that sent that man to the gallows.
I have no repentance for that advice. I certainly would have most absolutely failed in my duty, and colleagues would have failed equally with me, had we given any other advice. Should we have sent it forth broadcast throughout this country that all that the burglar and the man willing to murder in the process of burglary has to do to save his neck, is to secure a companion so that you will not know which of the two did the shooting, when those who seek to interfere with him in the perpetration of his crimes have been murdered? I say it is an absolutely salutary law. If a guilty man ever went to the gallows, and I now have in mind the man who did not fire the

shot, I say it was that mail. So much for that one particular instance which the hon. member has been able to point out in which he says an innocent man went to the gallows.

maintopic: FIRST CANADIAN CONTINGENT- SUPPLY OF CARTRIDGES.
speechtext: I did not say an innocent man. I said he was innocent of the crime for which he was condemned and hanged. I will say he was a bad man.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: FIRST CANADIAN CONTINGENT- SUPPLY OF CARTRIDGES.
speechtext:
I do not know that it makes any material difference. This is his statement as " Hansard " reported ft, although of course I am quite willing to take the hon. gentleman's statement and believe the reporter was in error. I will read it just to show that certainly I did not intentionally misquote the hon. gentleman. He is reported as having said:
Another reason why capital punishment should be abolished is that innocent men are sometimes executed. We know of one innocent man who was hanged in Canada, and we have grave doubts that there were not three innocent men hanged.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier: Who were they?
Mr. Bickerdike: One innocent man that we know of was hanged in New Westminster, B.C.
That is the innocent man I have been speaking of. Now, the hon. gentleman referred to another case not as an instance of where an innocent man had been hanged, but apparently for the purpose of showing how horrifying was the execution of the death penalty. He told us of an unfortunate man who was hanged at Calgary, and pictured the distressing circumstances of that man's death. It would appear that the man was cut down before he was actually dead and that it took some little period of time-I think that the hon. gentleman said twenty minutes-before life was entirely extinct. I believe that was the fact, and it certainly was a most distressing circumstance for those whose duty it was to be present and witness what happened. But, if I am not mistaken, the very best authorities say that a man, having undergone what he underwent, is unconscious absolutely from the moment that the drop falls. It is very distressing that that should have happened, but there are good and innocent men who die under greater suffering every day. Undoubtedly, it would be a horrible thing if the law provided that any unnecessary suffering should be imposed upon a man who had to be executed. For my part, I do not think that I am much more hard-hearted than the average man, but if it did happen that a condemned man suffered some of the agony that hundreds of thousands of innocent men suffer on their dying beds, I do not know that to avoid that we would be justified in wiping out that, which in my conviction is, to say the least of it, an invaluable aid to society in the discharge of its duty to protect human life.
We have had some statistics put before us for the purpose of supporting the proposition that the infliction of capital punishment does, not deter people from committing crime. If I correctly seize the purpose for which these statistics are cited, it is to lead us to the conclusion that because in some of the countries where there is capital punishment there have been as many or more murders as in other countries where there is no capital punishment, the infliction of capital punishment does not deter people from committing crime. Other statistics are cited for the purpose of showing that in some countries, at a period when capital punishment prevailed, there were as many, or more, murders as there have been since capital punishment was abolished. As regards the first class of statistics, you have to consider a great many other things, when you are comparing two countries, than the mere matter of whether capital punishment prevails in one and not in another. There are a great many things tKat render probable the commission of crimes of a certain class that might exist in one country and not in another. If you have a wild, unsettled, or only partially settled country, where the methods for the detection of crime are weak, and where the opportunity for escape.is ready to the hand of the criminal, you have circumstances that render it probable that you will have more crime in that country than in an adjacent, well-settled, quiet country, where the arm of the law is strong and reaches the offender easily. If in that latter country there was no capital punishment, and if in the former there was, if murders are more numerous in the former country, and if you are to be guided by statistics alone, you say:	Why,
it is the presence of capital punishment that apparently incites to murder. I want to show how absolutely unconclusive mere statistics are when dealing with a question of this kind. If you take them for the purpose of showing that in some country, at a period when capital punishment prevailed, murders were numerous, while at a later period when capital punishment had disappeared murders are few, you have to consider the advance of civilization within the country, and the possible change of conditions. It is a most dangerous thing to say

that purely and simply because after capital punishment was abolished murders did not
increase or that they even decreased capital punishment does not deter. Post hoc, ergo propter* hoc was always one of the most dangerous of arguments. They say, the devil can quote Scripture to support his own propositions.
You might quote statistics also to show that capital punishment should not be abolished if statistics are to settle the question. In 1905, comparative statistics of murder in the United Kingdom, where capital punishment prevails, and in Italy, where there is no capital punishment, were gathered. It was found that, whereas in the United Kingdom the murders were 25 or 26 for every million persons, in Italy where there was no capital punishment the murders were 105 for every million persons. If statistics are to settle this matter, there is a very startling argument indeed. I do not contend that they do. I quite admit that *in that case, as in the other case to which I have referred, you have to look into a great many other conditions prevailing in the respective countries; but I mention it as showing that after all statistics may be appealed to on both sides of this question.
While we are on statistics I would like to call attention to some that come right home to ourselves, and that I think have a particular bearing upon this question. Within the last few years we have had a most alarming increase in the number of *murders in this country. If you go back over a period of ten or twelve years, you will find that we had an average of twelve or thirteen convictions for murders per annum, whereas in the last three years the figures have been 26, 24, and I think 29 respectively, or in all 79 convictions for murder in Canada in the past three years. Tn that connection I would like to call attention to the fact that out of those 79 convictions for murder 38 were convictions of foreigners newly arrived in this country. Of those 38 foreigners 27 were people wlio came to us from countries where capital punishment either had been entirely abolished, or at all events was not applicable to the ordinary case of murder. That means that of our murders 49 per cent were committed by people newly arrived amongst us, and that of that 49 per cent, 68 per cent were committed by men who came from *countries where capital punishment had been abolished or at all events did not-apply to the ordinary crime , of murder. Can we have any better lesson5

maintopic: FIRST CANADIAN CONTINGENT- SUPPLY OF CARTRIDGES.
speechtext: I think that is a pretty good argument in my favour.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: FIRST CANADIAN CONTINGENT- SUPPLY OF CARTRIDGES.
speechtext:
I am glad if my hon friend is satisfied with the argument. I am satisfied with it. The hon. member does not bear in mind how relatively small a proportion of our population this foreign element is, and yet they contribute 49 per cent of our murders, and 68 per cent of that 49 per cent, or 35 per cent of our entire murders, are committed by people who come from those countries where capital punishment does not prevail or is not applicable to the particular crime of murder. It seems to me that it establishes beyond a doubt that among that class of people you see the absence of the constant pressure resulting upon the minds of the whole community from the fact that murder is put aside in that class by itself as the crime that calls for death. Certainly it is no unfair thing to say that it is evidence that those people look more lightly on human life, to the sacredness of which the hon. member attaches such importance, than do the great bulk of cur population who have grown up under this awful shadow of the death sentence being imposable upon murderers. The same thing is true when you look at the comparison between the people who come from countries where capital punishment prevails and those who come from countries where it does not prevail.-Those statistics seem to me to have a direct bearing upon this question.
Is it an opportune time to mate the change proposed when murder is becoming additionally frequent amongst us, and when we find that it is additionally frequent because we are getting flooded with a population who are accustomed to think that vou can kill your neighbour but that your life is so sacred that the state will never touch you? It seems to me that this is not the time to adopt the system that prevails in the countries from which these people come to us, who have such a light idea of the value of human life. Perhaps as the years go by, and when we all get better trained and more advanced (as I suppose the hon. gentleman would say), when the horror of murder shall have been more impressed upon the universal human mind, it may perhaps then be possible to withdraw the means or the method whereby it was so impressed; but until that time comes, and so long as we live in a country where we find that we are being flooded with people who have grown up so careless of human life under a state of law that was so careful of the lives of the guilty that it forgot to take care of the lives of the innocent, we may very well adhere to the safe old rule that

has come down to us from our fathers, to the rule that has behind it the sanction of human law for centuries, jmd that has behind it the sanction of the divine law.
The hon. member, if I am not mistaken, asserted absolutely that there was no country that had ever abolished capital punishment and that had gone back to it.
I would like to point out to the hon. gentleman his mistake in that respect. I have been at some pains to get absolutely accurate information, and it shows that in quite a number of countries capital punishment has been abolished and people have come back to it, and that in some of those countries they have abolished it again, and in some of them they have adhered to it. That has happened in Austria-Hungary; that has happened in seven or eight of the states in Germany. Capital punishment was abolished in Brunswick, Coburg, Nassau, Oldenburg in 1849; Saxe-Meiningen, Saxe - Weimar in 1862; Baden in 1863, and Saxony in 1868. In 1872, it was restored by the Imperial Criminal Code, limited, it is true, to attempts on the life of the emperor or the sovereign of any State, deliberate homicide as opposed to unintentional homicide, and treasonable acts. Here we have a noteworthy case of repeal followed by re-establishment. In Russia capital punishment was abolished in 1750 and subsequently reenacted, and freely inflicted. Since 1907, there his been no capital punishment in Russia, it is true, save for crimes endangering the life of the Emperor .or Empress or the heir to the throne. In Switzerland no less than seven of the Cantons in which capital punishment was abolished have since returned to it. In the United States you have the cases of Rhode Island and Colorado which states returned to capital punishment after having abolished it. Maine is another instance of the same kind. It is true, some	of	these	states have	sinceabolished it again. But, so far as the hon. gentleman seems to find what he regards	as	an	unanswerable	argument in	the	fact	that those	statesthat have	abolished	capital punishment
have never repented their action, I think these instances are enough to show that his assertion is, at all events too wide. I do not intend to detain the House at any greater length upon the merits of this question. I have tried to put forward the reasons which lead me to conclude that the House should reject the measure the hon. gentleman has proposed.
There is one matter, perhaps not directly
pertinent to this discussion but which has been introduced into it by one of the hon. gentlemen who spoke on Monday evening during my absence, the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards). I once knew a distinguished alienist who said that all men and women were on their way either to the penitentiary or to the insane asylum. When he was remonstrated with, he said that he could not qualify that statement further than to say* that some people died before they got there. Now, it rather seems to me that, from wherever I start or for wherever I start, I am gently led up to both the penitentiary and the insane asylum. That is the predicament in which I find myself now. However, I have no fault to find with the hon. member because he has led me up to the consideration of these two institutions. I have every sympathy with every one who is anxious about the condition of our penitentiaries, and more particularly about the manner of treatment of our unfortunate insane convicts. I have every sympathy with him, because I share his anxiety. It is a subject that is present to my mind during a very large part of the time, and which has given me matter for thought, and I may say for action, during a period of months. The argument of the hon. member with regard to this Bill-though I understood him not to support the measure-was that there were worse things than hanging, because a man might be sent to Kingston penitentiary. He went on to tell us the reason why he said that. Now, I want to deal with this thing frankly, fairly, and quite calmly- for it is altogether too big a question to afford room for anything in the nature of personal feeling, and I am quite sure that the hon. gentleman who made the observations to which I am going to refer will agree witih me in that. But he made these statements, and they are very grave. Certainly, whatever one may think of their value as an argument bearing on the infliction of capital punishment, they are altogether too grave to be allowed to go to the public unanswered. I desire purely and simply to answer these statements so far as they are statements of fact. When referring to the case to which the hon. member who proposed the Bill instanced, that of a man said to be innocent, at all events, of the offence of which he was convicted, but who was hanged, the hon. member for Frontenac said:
But supposing only one of them had heen hanged, and that the other had heen mercifully

Unfortunately there is not sufficient work to employ all the inmates otherwise; consequently we have to keep a large gang breaking stone. The stone pile, however, Is the last resort. Those working in the tailor and shoe shops and in other sedentary occupations are given exercise ''a the fresh air morning and afternoon. The prison of isolation is used solely for gross breaches of prison discipline. Except in rare rases the term of confinement is about three months.

speechtext:
Does the warden inform the hon. minister what proportion of the total number of inmates work on the stone pile?
M,r. DOHERTY: No, he has not sent me that information. The stone pile is not a pleasant or desirable place, and I shall be glad when it becomes possible to find work for all these men without putting them on the stone pile, but I venture to say that work on the stone pile is better than enforced idleness. However, I do not want to argue; I want to put the fact?, as I have every confidence they exist, before this House -and before the public. The hon. gentleman further makes this assertion:
He is subjected to tauntings and goadings and torturings, and if he rebels against them he is taken to a specially-constructed cell, a nose pressure of 70 pounds is turned on the poor unfortunate wretch; and he is thrown and knocked "bout in the cell until, as they say, he gives in.
Bear in mind that it is stated that these things occur at the present time. The report of the warden goes on to deal with matters which do not bear upon the subject under discussion, but I will read them to show that I do not want to conceal anything :
There are two men who have been confined in this building for about three years, for the reason that it would be a menace to the safety of the prison to permit them to be at large with the other prisoners. These are two of the five men who succeeded in escaping from this building about three years ago, after almost killing Guard Davis and seriously injuring two other officers. The other three men implicated in the escape were less dangerous characters, and have been at work for some time. So far as I am aware there are no ' tauntings ' or ' goadings ' of prisoners by officers. Needless to say if such a thing came to my knowledge it would entail the suspension of the officers and a recommendation that he be dismissed. No prisoner has b >n hnee: since I have been in charge or for some time before.
Mr. Creighton has been in charge, if my memory is correct, since some time last May. He was there as acting warden for a period of time prior to his actual appointment as warden, and I have information, of which I have not the slightest doubt, that for at least two years there has been no hosing, and under his predecessor in



office. Col. Irvine, my information is that there has been no hosing, and in any event we are dealing with conditions at the present time. As I said, I gave instructions that care was to be taken, pending whatever might be considered to be the final determination of what ought to be accepted or what ought not to be accepted in the report of the investigation, to avoid the outstanding things that they condemned, and this hosing has not taken place and does not take place at the present time. I do not wish to be carried back to any discussion of the past, hut I think it fair to say that any generalization by which it would be understood that any man who came into the penitentiary would at any period probably be hosed, would not be borne out by the evidence before the investigation. But cases were found, and the larger number occurred while the penitentiary was under the administration of a gentleman who was not the permanent regular warden of the penitentiary. However, it will be wiser to adhere to conditions at the present time, because it is present conditions that are in question in the observations of the hon. gentleman, and because no good purpose would be served by going hack over the past, save in so far as we may find in it a lesson to guide our conduct in the future.
The next statement of the hon. member for Frontenac is:
If that treatment sends him into the hospital, on Sunday he gets three meals, the first at nine o'clock, the next at eleven o'clock, and the third at one o'clock in the afternoon.
The statement of the warden is:
In the hospital the meals on Sunday are served at, approximately, the following hours: breakfast, 8.15; dinner, 1 p.m.; supper, 4 p.m. During the week the supper hour varies with the closing hour of the prison. This, however, we are trying to rearrange; it requires thought and consideration to bring about the change without endangering the safety of the prison. When patients are seriously ill they receive constant attention, and are given nourishment day and night, as ordered by the surgeon.

speechtext:
I have seen a large number of things published in the papers that were not borne out by the facts.
The warden further says:
When prisoners are seriously ill they receive constant attention, and are given nourishment

day and night, as ordered by the surgeon. I may say that during the present fiscal year, which will expire on March 31, there have been but two deaths, not a high average with a population of over 500 inmates.
There were two deaths in that period of time; whether they are the two to which the hon. member referred it is impossible for me to say; but as the hon. mem-
9 p.m. ber tells me that it has been stated that two men died there utterly unattended, I shall inquire into that situation. The warden continues:
During the winter months the inmates of me asylum, with the exception of two or three, who have marked homicidal tendencies and are of necessity kept in their cells, spend the day in a large room provided for that purpose and there means of recreation, such as draughts and playing cards, are afforded.

That is in connection with the statement that:
They tear it to pieces with their fingers and teeth like wild animals.

They are provided with spoons, but no forks, the latter being used in the prison proper only. Tubbing, if it ever listed, has been a thing of the past for a long period.
That is in reference to the statement:
If any one of them dares to utter a protest against one of the guards or keepers, the unfortunate wretch is stripped, specially . constructed harness is fastened on him, his legs are bound together and his arms fastened to his side and he is dipped into a tub of ice-cold water, being left there until, as they say, he gives in.
That is the statement of the present warden of the penitentiary with regard to the conditions. As I say, I believe the gentleman to be trustworthy and reliable, and, with regard to the statement he makes to me of the conditions, they indicate the carrying out of instructions that were given and insisted upon.

speechtext: The hon. member the other afternoon did not refer to that, and therefore I did not inquire; but I shall be very glad to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: FIRST CANADIAN CONTINGENT- SUPPLY OF CARTRIDGES.
speechtext:
I believe that is true. The warden, however, has made the statement of the facts. There is a further observation I desire to make with regard to the treatment of the insane. The hon. member, of course, will hardly expect that I. will agree with him in his observations as to the Minister of Justice. Of course, he is fully entitled to appreciate my conduct as it presents itself to his view, and I have no desire to quarrel with him on the subject. At the same time, he will not expect me to agree in his observations on that subject. He says:
That it was three years ago when he first directed my attention to this condition of affairs at Kingston penitentiary and Kingston penitentiary is probably no better than other penitentiaries in the country.
My memory is not in accord with the memory of the hon. member, but I have no desire to quarrel about that. His position in the matter or mine is of relatively small importance as compared with the importance of the work at the penitentiary. As regards the treatment of the insane, I want to add something which may have a bearing on my alleged apathy in that regard.
The Commissioners found that conditions at the insane hospital were not suitable, and recommended-I am not pretending to quote their words-that these people should be in an institution provided for the insane, and suggested that this might be done under the provincial authorities. I took the matter up very shortly after last session and came to the conclusion that the proper course, when it would be possible to do it, would be for this Government to provide a special institution for the detention of insane convicts. I have no hesitation in saying that in my opinion it is not a desirable way to deal with persons who are insane, whether convicts or not, to keep them in an insane asylum carried on as an adjunct to a penitentiary.
But of course you cannot create an institution of that kind in a day, and I looked for a more prompt method of action, for something that might temporarily meet what is quite clear to me is a need. I took the matter up with the provincial governments. Under the existing condition of affairs in the provinces of British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba, insane convicts are taken care of in insane asylums by the provincial authorities. This had been done under arrangement with the provincial governments. Under the Penitentiary Act we are authorized to deal with insane convicts in one of two ways;
18*
either by the establishment and maintenance of an insane ward; or by having them sent to provincial insane asylums under an arrangement made for that purpose with the lieutenant-governor. When this Government came in we found an insane ward in existence at Kingston which had been used for a considerable period of time, and to which insane convicts from the provinces of Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, and I believe from the Yukon, were sent. Such was the system we found in existence. As the result of our own examination, I might perhaps say to some extent of my own examination, as well as in consequence of the views expressed by the Commissioners, 1 have reached the conclusion that that is not the best way to deal with these unfortunate people. Having that in mind, 1 took this matter up with the provincial governments shortly after the end of last session. I did not find that it was simply a matter of saying, will you do this? and their being prepared at once to say, yes. The matter was a serious one from their point of, view, and while at a very early period the Government of Quebec expressed their willingness to take over convicts from that province, they coupled with it what under their system they necessarily had to, a condition that we should make satisfactory arrangements with the proprietors of the insane asylums; for the system down there is a system of proprietary asylums subsidized by the Government, not a system of government institutions. In Ontario the Government was at first entirely indisposed to take over these patients because of the fact that they found themselves crowded in their present institutions. We had some correspondence on the subject, and I impressed upon these gentlemen the importance of this work and the consideration that it was a good work in the cause of humanity. After looking over the situation they consented to find means to provide for these men, and are at present classifying them at the institutions; for I understand they contemplate distributing these men in different institutions, as the case warrants. In the province of Quebec we have reached the point where the Government has expressed its consent subject to such conditions as I have mentioned, and there I hope arrangements will be completed in a few days. In New Brunswick, where we have only one man to deal with, the Provincial Government has consented to take him over and he

has been sent to them. So that we have kept at work preparing this great amelioration, and I hope soon to have it completed. I am free to admit that it might have gone quicker under different circumstances, but I fancy that everybody knows that the condition of this country since the war began, and the condition in which in consequence this Government has been placed, has necessitated delays with regard to many projects. But I am not here pleading any excuses, nor am I making any boasts whatever. The fact is that in common with my *colleagues the state of war since August last has created a condition where the time of myself and largely of the people in my department has had to be given to things that were of the first importance and called pressingly for immediate attention. If that situation had not existed this negotiation with regard to insane asylums might have been pushed with more vigour. I do not know that we should sooner have reached a conclusion, because of course it was a matter of persuading other people. Although the work might have gone on quicker in different circumstances, the delay is not for want of a real interest in the subject and a real determination to do the best that was possible to ameliorate the condition of these unfortunate people.
I have made what I deemed to be the necessary explanation to meet the very serious statements which the hon. member (Mr. Edwards) made the other evening. My conviction is that he is misinformed upon these .subjects. Further than that I have no comment to make upon his observations. I have no doubt that he acts believing in the -.truth of his statements and that he was doing his duty in making them. I equally have felt it my duty to meet them with the answer which I have given, and of the correctness of which I am absolutely convinced. In saying that, I am speaking of course of that portion of it which is not personal to myself. As to what has been done and is being done in regard to insane asylums, I speak of my own knowledge.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with a great deal of attention to the statements made this afternoon by the Hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), in respect to the Bill now before the House. I may say at the outset that I fully agree with what he said in regard to capital punishment.
In the course of the last session, the hon. member for St. Lawrence (Mr. Bickerdike) introduced a Bill to the same effect, and
[Mr. Doherty. J
after listening attentively to what he had to say, I found that I could not comply with his request that I should support his Bill; far from it, I felt bound to oppose it.
I was not at my seat when the hon. gentleman once more introduced the matter, but I have read the report of the speech he delivered on that occasion, and I must say that he did not bring in any. new arguments, and was content with going over his statements of last year. The reasons alleged previously, and which had failed to win me over to his point of view, have not met with greater success this year.
As was stated by the hon. Minister of Justice, this is a very serious question and which should be discussed most carefully, without show of prejudice or ill-feeling. When it comes to a question of amending the law inflicting capital punishment, and of repealing its provisions, very weighty reasons should be given to justify such a course. I have the greatest respect for the motives which have induced the hon. member for St. Lawrence to take such a stand. Satisfied that he is fulfilling a duty and doing what is right by his constituents, believing that such a change should be effected, he insists that his Bill should go through. I hasten to say that I believe him to be sincere and acting in good faith, though all the while mistaken. The hon. gentleman submitted to the House a carefully prepared and painstaking presentment of his case; but he will allow me to say that, had he a more intimate acquaintance with what is going on in our criminal courts, and specially in the district of Montreal, possibly he would not be so anxious to secure the repeal of an Act which, in my humble opinion, should remain in our statute-books.
Having enjoyed for the last nine years the signal honour of representing the Attorney General in the district of Montreal, I made it a point, Mr. Speaker, to look into the question, and did my best to satisfy myself that there was something good and useful in the measure introduced by the hon. member. But the older I get, the wider my experience, and the more I am satisfied, on the contrary, that it would be a grievouk mistake to abolish capital punishment.
The hon. gentleman referred to judicial errors. He spoke of the pity inspired by, of the mercy which should be shown to, those who murder their fellow creatures, and who are brought up for trial before the criminal courts. I also, Mr. Speaker, have feelings

of pity; I also have a heart, I also know that it is painful to condemn a fellow-being to death. But were the hon. gentleman to consider the question from the standpoint of the victims, possibly he would not be so anxious to secure the abolition of the death penalty in the case of those who, from then-own impulse, inflicted it on a fellow-citizen.
It is objected:	But why hang the man?
Would it not be enough to send him to penitentiary for life? Would not society, through such means be sufficiently safeguarded? I have had occasion to see how matters are in the penitentiaries. In 1897,
I was called upon to investigate at some length how things were being managed at the St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary. Numerous cases were at the time looked into, until I had obtained a fairly accurate knowledge of the situation. I tried to find out whether errors had not been committed prejudicial to those who were interned, some of them under sentences for life. I also tried to satisfy myself, as the hon. member for St. Lawrence has done, that life sentences in the penitentiaries afford sufficient and adequate protection for the community. Well, I must acknowledge that, as a result, I reached the very opposite conclusion. I found that criminals, though shut up for life in penitentiaries and I make particular reference at St. Vincent de Paul * were still a danger to the community, inasmuch as they were turned into professors for the teaching of crime.
Criminals serving life sentences in our penitentiaries are actually expert teachers in the arts of the criminal, who spend night and day plotting to make their fellow-prisoners even worse than they are. Is that the kind of protection that the hon. member for St. Lawrence would secure for the community? Such people spend the greater part of their lives in the penitentiaries in an effort to corrupt their fellow prisoners. I may state for the benefit of the hon. gentleman ' that criminals interned in our penitentiaries are the most dangerous people with whom the community has to deal. Society has a right to protect itself against them, and such criminals should be punished in proportion to their guilt.
Oh, but, the hon. gentleman may interpose, you are the Crown prosecutor, and therefore not in a position to express an unbiased opinion, considering that you are paid for doing such work. My answer is that I am no more prejudiced than he is himself, and that moreover, I always feel very sorry when, in the fulfilment of my
duties as Crown prosecutor, I must ask that the death penalty be inflicted on some of those poor fellows. I always feel sorry when I have to insist on the carrying out of the law against them. We, Crown prosecutors, are in duty bound to forward the ends of justice, not by any means to secure convictions under all circumstances, and we are always glad when lawyers for the defence can procure the release of their client and induce the jury to give a verdict of not guilty. The fees we are paid are not for the purpose of securing convictions, but solely with a view to forwarding the ends of justice. It is immaterial to us, as far as money is concerned, whether the charge is sustained or not. Should the ver-diet be one of not guilty, the Crown has no reason to be dissatisfied, since the accused has proved his innocence. A verdict of guilty is also a source of satisfaction to the Crown, since the majesty of the law is thereby upheld. Jurors are at all times warned to be careful before rendering a verdict of guilty to make sure that there is no possibility of error; should there subsist the least doubt, jurors are instructed that the accused should be given the benefit of it, for it is preferable that ninety-nine criminals should escape, rather than have one innocent person to suffer eondamn-ation. Such is our duty and we are careful to fulfill it conscientiously.
Reference has been made to judicial errors; it is an easy matter to dilate on such a subject, but much more difficult to prove one's statements. Now, in the course of the last ten years I have had constantly to do with the administraion of justice in ai* important district; in the meantime, numerous trials have taken place, many verdicts have been rendered, and once more I assert that not a single judicial error has been pointed out. It has been insinuated that such an error had been committed, but no evidence whatevver has been adduced in support of this contention. A single case has been suggested. It was claimed that a judicial error had been committed in the case of a man in whose behalf the intervention of the Government, was sought after he had undergone five or six years' detention in the penitentiary. His discharge was asked, but not on the ground of any judicial error. There was no reference to the subject in the solemn declaration. A petition was forwarded to the hon. Minister of Justice and the hon. gentleman deemed it proper to grant the discharge sought for. Is that any evidence

of the so called judicial error which has been referred to? No, there was no judicial error committed. What happened was only this, that the hon. minister considered that the prisoner had paid the penalty of his crime and took pity on him; nothing more. I am quite conversant with the case referred to, and I may say to the hon. minister that he was right in extending mercy under the circumstances, and in granting the petition forwarded to him, he did so of his own accord, and not on account of the discovery of any so-called judicial error. He then set at liberty a man who had been five or six years in the penitentiary.
Taking into account the safeguards provided by the requirements of the law in all criminal proceedings, it is not an easy matter that a judicial error should occur. To begin with, a complaint is filed with the magistrate who is not to finally dispose of the case but simply to decide whether there is a prima facie case against the accused, and should this be so, the latter is sent before the grand jury. Witnesses previously summoned before the magistrate will be called to testify a second time before the grand-jury, and the grand-jury in turn, inquires whether the prosecution should go on. Should the grand-jury bring in a true .bill, the accused will then have to appear before the petty jury, consisting of twelve of his peers, and they will render final 'judgment. The evidence is taken and the accused either convicted or discharged. Should the accused be a poor man, unable to secure the services of a lawyer, the .Crown immediately provides one for him. and if necessary summons witnesses in his behalf. Should he be found guilty, after being granted the full benefit of doubtful circumstances, the docket is completed and forwarded to the authorities who, in turn, will look into all the proceedings.
The record, then, is examined, so is the judge's charge, so is the evidence, and the judge is expected to forward a report to the Minister of Justice. Should all that prove insufficient, should there still be a doubt, the benefit of that doubt is given to the accused. Lastly, the prisoner may solicit the royal clemency. And, as an additional means, there are the writ of error and the writ of appeal. When new issues are raised by the accused, he has the right to demand that the full court of appeal should look into the records. And still, should he be not satisfied, he may take his case to the Supreme court and as far as the Privy Council in England.
fMr. Lafortune.]
All the aforesaid proceedings show how' jealously the rights of the accused are safeguarded, so that full and entire justice be meted out to him. Why then show' such compassion for those who are to suffer capital punishment? Why should they specially be the object of our pity?
Murderers do not kill for the mere pleasure of taking other people's life. Tney do so through a desire to plunder, rob, dispossess their victim of the treasures they covet. Murderers commit outrages, and then take the life of their victims, and dispossess their victim of the treasures They set fire to buildings, and then commit murder. Still there will be found people who take compassion on such ruffians and who are ready to blame others anxious that such crimes be punished by the infliction of the death penalty. They forget that these thugs have not taken compassion on their victims, that they have not even given them time to make their peace with God and clear their conscience before departing for the other life. Criminals, on the other hand, are granted all the time requisite to majse their peace with God, a privilege they withheld from their victims. How strange that so much goodly feeling should be expended on these cut-throats, while so little heed is paid to the sufferings of their victims.
There was a poor man, a workingman, settled in my village; he used to work in the quarries at Joliette. One day he started out with some tools, some clothes and twenty dollars in his valise. On his way he was murdered by some one who wanted to have that money and other valuables. Now, the hon. member for St. Lawrence tells us:	Hands off that murderer ! I say that all the people in my village were loud in their clamourings not for revenge, but for justice, anxious as they were that any others who might be tempted to follow in the lead of that cutthroat should, through the knowledge of the punishment inflicted, be deterred from doing so.
I shall point out another instance. A middle-aged man having met a young girl just leaving school, took her against her will into a house, and after outraging her, shoved her through a third-story window. Notwithstanding that, the hon. gentleman considers that this miscreant is entitled to mercy. I wonder what would have happened, supposing the hon. gentleman had been the father of that child. I am pretty sure that that would have caused him to change

his mind, and possibly he would have killed the man on the spot.
I may cite still another case. By dint of hard work and strict economy, a man had succeeded in saving $300. His intention was to send that money to Italy, his country of origin. One of his fellow-citizens, born in the same village, tried to induce a fellow-worker to accompany them both on a trip to the Cedars. His plan was to rob the other fellow and murder him, if need be, with the help of his friend. However, the latter refused, saying that rather than commit such a crime, he would prefer losing his own life. If we are to believe the hon. gentleman the man who started out to commit that crime single-handed was worthy of the concern of his fellow-citizens and should not have undergone capital punishment.
While, as I stated a moment ago, I respect the view held by the hon. member for St. Lawrence, but he must be ignorant of what is going on before the courts.
We are told that once the criminal is interned, the community will no longer run any risks. The hon. gentleman would have quite a different story to tell if he had inquired into the facts which occurred at the St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary in the year 1885-86, when the then warden, Dr. Laviolette, came near losing his life at the hands of some of the convicts serving life sentences and who had been for months engaged in a conspiracy to escape from the penitentiary. They would have attained their object, had it not been for the remarkable courage displayed by the warden who refused to give up the keys to these ruffians. They left him lying in the yard, and believing him to be dead, were content with killing two men and severely injuring a third. Such is the protection afforded by the penitentiary. Mainville,-I can speak freely of him to-day, since he is dead,-was at the time a recognized expert in the arts of the criminal.
During most every session of the Assize Court, convicts are brought from St. Vincent de Paul against whom very serious charges have been made for having wounded, sometimes deadly, the guards of the penitentiary.
Let me tell the honourable member that he is mistaken, and that those people do more harm than before, because their hatred toward authority is boundless.
The hon. member may re-introduce his Bill every session-it is his right to do so-but I do not think he will ever find a majority to sanction his request. As far as I am concerned, he must set forth some
more convincing reasons in order to have me change my opinion.
I say to the hon. member: You are not doing justice to the community by asking, with no argument whatever in support of your proposal, that we should do away with capital punishment. A poor man is slaughtered, his wife and children are plunged into the greatest misery as a consequence of that crime, and then you talk of charity, of humanity, of what a cruel thing it is to take away the life of a fellow man. But did the murderer allow his victim to prepare for death, to set his temporal and spiritual concerns in order? No, he struck him treacherously, without giving him one moment for reflection, whereas he, the murderer, will have months and months to prepare his departure from this life, in view of the life to come.
The hon. Minister of Justice was quite right in saying, a moment ago, that the most dangerous culprits are those interned in the penitentiaries. Most of the strangers who become guilty of such heinous crimes are from countries where capital punishment has been abolished. I have examined the record of some of these prisoners, and I could not believe my eyes when I witnessed that a man had only been sentenced to six months' imprisonment for having once committed murder, and to nine months for the same offence in another instance. Is it strange that such individuals, when in our country, should kill so readily? No, because such is their frame of mind. They think that the same treatment is awaiting them here as in their own country, and that they will get no more than six months' imprisonment for one murder and nine months for another.
The session of March will soon be opened. Indeed, there is a great increase in the number of crimes, but that increase would be still greater were the hon. member for St. Lawrence to have his Bill approved by this House. We could no longer allow our wives and children to go out and walk on the streets of our great cities after six o'clock in the evening, nor even by full daylight, lest they should be attacked. Is it not true that things so happened in the case of Hayden, who slaughtered a child in order to rob him of eleven cents? Yes, he struck him with his knife and left him dead on the sidewalk. And the hon. member tells us that we should have pity on that man, on that murderer? Really, I cannot believe my ears.

I am only quoting those several cases from memory; but how many crimes,are committed which will remain forever unknown and unpunished, notwithstanding the severity of the law? Who does not recollect the case of Gregoire? A man knocked a poor woman down on Jaeques-Cartier street at three o'clock in the afternoon, to rob her of five dollars; he had pounded her with a bottle and had left her as dead on the street. And we should have pity on that man? Who does not recollect also the case of Demers which created such a sensation at the time, the murderer in that case, having never been detected? The poor woman was found weltering in her blood, at six o'clock in the morning. And the case of Quinn? Somebody had murdered a poor old woman who lived alone in her house, in order to take $100 away from her; the corpse was found, cut to pieces, at four o'clock in the afternoon.
Let us extend our protection to thieves and murderers, when no later than last winter, at St. Laurent, in my own village, Beauchamp, Bourret and Foucault, who had just stolen a few flitches of meat at a butcher's stall in the village, killed two policemen who were trying to arrest them, for we all know that robbers are always provided with the tools they want for the purpose of committing murder. Let us protect those assassins, let us have pity on them, let us ask that the law be repealed, let us apply to those poor murderers the law of Christ which forbids that they should be hanged, because this would be contrary to humanity. Well, as far as I am concerned, I say that the assassins and the -murderers should behave honestly, and they would by no means be endangered. But so long as the law of Christ demands that justice should be done, so long as humanity remains what it is, let us apply this precept: Eye for eye, tooth for tooth. He who draws the sword shall perish by the sword. If you wish to be respected, you should first have respect for others.
The motives of these culprits are always the same: Bobbery, plunder and rape.
When a prisoner comes before us and is found guilty of a mere manslaughter, never is he hanged. The Crown must prove that there was malice and premeditation, in order that an execution should take place.
If the Crown failed to establish that the murder was committed deliberately, with malice, and premeditation, the verdict should always be to the effect that there was manslaughter only.

It was said before to-night, and justly so, that the assassins should first refrain from committing murder, and hanging would then be done away with. But until the assassins have done so, I see no reason why our laws providing for capital punishment should be amended. It has been suggested that we should make an experiment; the hon. member urged us to repeal the law, and he suggested that, should this measure fail to give good results, we could at any rate, have capital punishment restored. But the same experience was made in other countries; in France, for instance, the system advocated by the hon. member was resorted to. The guillotine was abolished, and what was the result? Crimes increased in number to such an alarming extent that the guillotine had to be restored. Why should we put ourselves in such a danger, I pray? Why should we make such a trial? Why should such a sad experience repeat itself in our country? I shall go no further, I have said enough already to make myself understood and to give an account of the experience I have acquired before the criminal courts.
I respect the opinion of the hon. member, but I think he is mistaken in requesting us to adopt such a Bill, a Bill which would bring about an intolerable condition of things, especially at this time, exposed as we are to receive here a great number of strangers as a consequence of what is taking place in other countries. In fact, we may well fear that with the influx of immigration which will come to our country hereafter and settle within our walls, a great number of these culprits may be found whom capital punishment alone could deter from committing such heinous crimes.
Let me tell the mayor of Montreal, who is sitting by my side, that he would not remain in his chair, as mayor of that great city, for a very long time were we to adopt this Bill. Owing to the official position which he holds, he is not a single day without receiving all kinds of threats from miscellaneous vagabonds, and were not the scaffold there, ready to throttle these misbelievers, they would soon put their threats into effect and kill him. The sentiments of the hon. member call for our respect, but he also must respect the opinion of those who think otherwise than he does. We are interested in the sound administration of justice to the same extent as he is, and that is the reason why we take leave to

differ in opinion with him on such a serious question.
I think I would be neglecting my duty as member for Montcalm should I fail to follow the dictates of my conscience, enlightened as it is by the experience I have acquired before the assizes of Montreal, and were I not to vote against the Bill now before us.
