speechtext:
I presume that
I am expected to make some reply to the very many criticisms-and some of them are rather unjust-which have been offered since I introduced this proposed amendment to the Criminal Code. I do not think my hon. friend from Montcalm (Mr. Lafortune) is a very fair witness in this case. He has had a great, big harvest out of sending souls into eternity, I suppose no bigger harvest than he has had in 1914, and he is expecting a very large one in 1915. He has grown fat, lusty and wealthy on send mg souls into eternity without caring where they are going to. It is generally stated that the hon. gentleman has made $50,000 out of sending souls into eternity. I shall not reply to the hon. gentleman any further than that. I say that he is an interested party. He wants the law, he wants the murders, and he wants to send the murderers to the other world. I would like to say one or two words in regard to the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards). While he was opposed to this Bill, he gave reasons for his opposition and these are the very reasons I advance in support of it. He said that it would be more of a punishment to send a man to Kingston penitentiary than to hang him. That is what I have contended all along. My hon. friend, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) argued rather in that direction too. He said that the loss of liberty was a greater punishment to the individual than the taking of his life. That is also exactly what I have been contending for. That is the principle upon which I have founded this Bill. If you want to punish a man and to provide a deterrent, I say it is a greater deterrent to send him to penitentiary, with the consequent loss of liberty, than that he should lose his life, and if that is the case let us abolish capital punishment.

maintopic: FIRST CANADIAN CONTINGENT- SUPPLY OF CARTRIDGES.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman made out a very strong case for you.

maintopic: FIRST CANADIAN CONTINGENT- SUPPLY OF CARTRIDGES.
speechtext:
be proved to be really necessary and indis-pensible, is contrary to the profession of Christianity. That is the- ground I stand on here. The question again resolves itself into proof, and I think I have already shown that the punishment of death is useless and unnecessary.
The security of life in Canada does not depend upon the public strangling of a few poor wretches every year, and I should be glad indeed that it might be said of this Government and this Parliament at some future time that it had dared to act upon the true lessons and not upon the superstitions of the past, and that it might be declared to be the Parliament which destroyed the gallows in order that it might teach that human life is sacred, for upon that alone can the public safety be secured. Reference has been made to the hanging of a poor unfortunate negro, the first criminal to be hanged on the new gallows at Bordeaux, and I may say here that the general impression is that poor Campbell was hanged innocent, at least so far as the crime for which he suffered is concerned. I do not mean to say, that he was an innocent man; he was a bad man, a poor man, a black man, he had no friends, and therefore he was hanged. Just before leaving the cell, in company with the Catholic priest, he wrote this illiterate and mis-spelled letter:	.
This is the word to let them know I died for nothing, before God and man I am not guilty of this crime, it was all made up on me
by	and the detectives. Really I am not
guilty of what I am accused. I want all coloured men not to take up with white women for God's sake, goodby.
(Signed) William Campbell,
in death cell.
He was just leaving his cell with his father confessor, to step into eternity, and this is what he said. He was hanged on January 24, 1914-my hon. friend from Montcalm knows all about it-for the murder of George Muir, at Senecal station on the Park and Island railway.
I wonder if the judge and the jury and my hon. friend the Crown Prosecutor and his running mate the Crown Executioner realize that they will have to stand on that last great Judgment Day side by side with these poor criminals whom they have sent into eternity. It is well to think upon these things at times. I have no doubt that the Minister of Justice will realize that also in regard to that poor man in British Columbia whom he sent into eternity, for which act he takes all the responsibility. I submit that where the equities are equal the

element of mercy should hold the balance of power in deciding this question; and with the statistics which I have given the House all the members ought to be convinced that the equities are equal, and that they will vote for mercy instead of blood for blood.
My hon. friend has given half a dozen pictures. Let me give just one-of the awful suffering and remorse of the family of the victim of the homicide. We agree that it is hard on the family of the deceased and our sympathy goes out to them whether death i,s the result of assassination or of justifiable homicide. It is just the same in either case. But for that reason would you have two widows, two sets of orphans and two sorrowing parents? Why, the family of the prisoner are just as innocent of an offence as the family of the deceased, and are just as much entitled to compassion and sympathy. For example, a man commits murder. He probably got drunk or was by environment made a criminal. He has a good wife and also children; a good mother and father and a large number of relatives, all innocent people and profoundly grieved that the offence was committed. The accused is tried and convicted and sentenced to be hanged. The very thought of taking the life of the husband, father, brother and son breaks a multitude of hearts. The time nas healed the wounds that grief for the victim rent; but as the days roll by and the time approaches for the execution of the prisoner, the hearts of the mother anu father all but break; the affectionate and tender cord of love that stretches from the altar to the scaffold is crushed but not broken, and the heart of the wife once gay is burned to its very socket. She goes to and from the awful death cell. Little innocent hearts of children are crushed like the tender blades of grass beneath the angry wheels of oannon on the German battlefield, yet they are all innocent. The brother and sister suffer for his sins, and see his ghost-like form in their dreams of repose. As the day draws near, the father and mother with tottering footsteps visit the death cell, and their minds wander back to the time when a little boy said his prayers at his mother's knee and whistled the tune that his father carrolled, and they ask God why they have this affliction to bear. The wife, children and relatives and friends all bid him goodby and leave with breaking hearts, bitterly thinking of to-morrow. With heartbreaking despair, the mother prays God to spare her child, and as the time flies by, the height of Heaven could not measure her

sorrow. The father's hair turns gray over night, and their very souls are all scarred and forever seared over by the thought of the vengeance visited on their unfortunate relative, son and husband and father. The parents are hurried to their graves of broken hearts; the wife tries to forget, but cannot forgive and the hearts of the children, relatives and friends are hardened by the harrowing example of killing by the country. Two families are in mourning and the prisoner's family crushed and heart-broken by a protracted suspense, and that amounts to cruelty to the innocents. Then why make two families instead of one desolate? Then suppose he was innocent? The country cannot retract what it has done. If life imprisonment would serve the same purpose, would you not prefer it to the death penalty? My hon. friend the Minister of Justice says it is a greater deterrent than the death penalty. Then why not abolish the death penalty?
One of the strongest arguments why capital punishment should be abolished is that innocent men are sometimes executed, and I will give a few instances. Some time ago Sir James McIntosh, a most calm and dispassionate observer, declared that, taking a long period of time, one innocent man was hanged in England every three years. I have no doubt my good friends the Minister of Justice and the hon. member for Montcalm will say:	What is one man in
three years; let him go; he will hardly be missed.
The late Chief Baron Kelly stated, as the result of his experience, that from 1802 to 1840, no fewer than twenty-two innocent men had been sentenced to death in England, of whom seven were actually executed. That is a point that apparently my opponents have forgotten. I wonder how my hon. friend will feel when he sends an innocent man into eternity?

speechtext:
It is pretty nearly as good as yours. Here is an opinion that the Crown Prosecutor will approve. Mrs. Booth says:
I know a man who has served nine years and is still in prison, where he has been visited by the hoy whom he was supposed to have murdered. The fact that in our day justice may thus miscarry must give men constant pause
before they seek remedial vengeance in the death penalty.
My opponents have handled the question altogether on the line of vengeance-a man has committed murder and we must kill him.
Mr. Scruggs, former secretary to ex-Governor Patterson, states on his honour that, while he was serving as said ex-Governor's secretary, an innocent negro was hanged, as it developed subsequent to the hanging.
Two negroes by the name of Duvall and 'Clapp were arrested for rape on a white woman by the name of Warden. She could not state whether her assailants were white or black. They tried, convicted and hanged the two negroes at Blandville, Ky. Their last words were that they were innocent of the crime. Some years later a white man by the name of Gossop moved to Arkansas from Milburn, and shortly afterwards took sick, and on his deathbed made confession to the crime. But two innocent lives had gone to meet their Maker. Let me give a few names that I know will be familiar to my friend. Socrates, Cicero, Sir Walter Raleigh, Algernon Sidney, John Huss, Michael Servetus, Louis XVI, the Due d'Enghien, Marshall Ney, Riego, Sandor Nagi, Maximilian, are among the conspicuous instances of victims of the law of blood.
I will now cite a case that I think the Minister of Justice knows something about as well as the hon. member for Montcalm. The most powerful case cited by Mr. Mc-Connico was the Durand case, from California. Durand, though ably defended, was convicted of the murder of his sweetheart in the tower of a church; and, on what appeared, so far as human eye could see, an absolutely perfect and unbreakable case of circumstantial evidence, he was convicted and hanged. About a year after the murder, the minister of the church in which the murder occurrred confessed that he was guilty of the crime for which the other man had been put to death.

speechtext: Have you the confession?

maintopic: FIRST CANADIAN CONTINGENT- SUPPLY OF CARTRIDGES.
speechtext:
No, I have not been there for some time. My hon. friend painted a very brilliant picture of a man robbing another of twenty dollars. I think that man deserved punishment, and I would not care how much you punished him, if you did not send his soul into eternity unprepared. And I want to say, that any man who really believes in the eternity of the soul will not vote for capital punishment-he cannot do it.

My hon. friend the Minister of Justice said, I think, that we had divine authority for capital punishment. He did not tell us where he found it. From Genesis to Revelation there is no commandment, no recommendation, of capital punishment. In fact, the Creator proved that he was in favour of the life penalty as against the death penalty. I was surprised when the Minister of Justice made that statement. Of course, he would not have made it had he not believed it; but I think it will be very difficult for him to establish it. Let me point out where you will find a very strong contradiction of the belief that we have divine authority for sending these poor souls into eternity. When Cain slew Abel-and that was the first murder we read about-God was the only arbiter between men. He was both the political and moral governor of men. Did God kill Cain? On the contrary, he gave him a life sentence, the very thing 1 am asking for:
When thou tillest the ground it shall not henceforth yield unto thee her strength; a fugitive and a vagabond shalt thou be in the earth.
And He added, in order to prevent another murder:
Whosoever slayeth Cain, vengeance shall be taken on him seven fold.
Could anything be clearer than that? I repeat, I challenge the Minister of Justice or any other member of this House to find a single word in Scripture, in the word of God, from Genesis to Revelations, that approves of capital punishment. No such word can be found.
The Minister of Justice said that he knew of some places that had abolished capital punishment, and reinstated it. I do not like to contradict the hon. gentleman, but I am sure he is in error. I say it boldly, there is no place in the world to-day that has once abolished capital punishment and is practising it to-day. Some places have abolished capital punishment and then reinstated it. But only for a short time. I say I do not wish to directly contradict the minister, if he has proof of his statement. But I have written to all these different countries, and in every case I have an answer that they are not practising capital punishment now. That is true of twenty-nine places. We had twenty-eight places when this Bill was up last year, but since -then New South Wales has adopted my very Bill. If these places find that abolition of capital punishment is best, and if the people there are satisfied, surely the Minister of Justice

and the Crown Prosecutor will not attempt to show that those people should be dissatisfied. These people say, in effect, that the abolition of capital punishment has reduced crime; were it otherwise they would go back to capital punishment.
I wish to tell the Minister of Justice that the day will come when he will introduce this Bill; he will get credit for it, and that will be all right. I should be glad if he would adopt the Bill and take the credit for it now; I had hoped until recently that he would accept the Bill as a Government measure.
I had intended laying a lot of statistics before the House; but the hour is late, and I will finish by giving one more picture- it is a picture that many hon. members have seen. A French painter has depleted this scene: In the dreary hours of night, Napoleon's drummer boy is made to arise and sound the march. The ghost of Napoleon comes forward and stands at attention. And then the Grand Army and the Old Guard pass by in solemn review before the " Archangel of War." They come from Areola, from Lodi, from Austerlitz, from Waterloo. And on Napoleon's face you see an expression which says as plainly as words: Is it possible that I am responsible for all these men being sent into eternity?
How many men have been burned at the stake, for their religious convictions-and surely religious conviction is no crime, whether we agree with it or not. Hundreds and hundreds have been burnt, some because they would not turn Protestant, some because they would not turn Catholic. As you are considering the passing of this law, the blood of the many martyrs of the block, the guillotine and the gibbet appeal to you to abolish the law that is founded on vengeance and destruction instead of on mercy and reform.
Motion for second reading of Bill negatived on division.

speechtext:
Mr. GEORGE E. McCRANEY (Saskatoon) moved the second reading of Bill No. 19, to amend the Criminal Code. He said:	.
This Bill is to amend Section 390 of the Criminal Code, which is as follows:
livery one is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to seven years' imprisonment who, being a trustee of any property for the use or benefit, either in whole or in part, of some other person, or for any public or charitable purpose, with intent to defraud, and in violation of his trust, converts anything of which he is trustee to any use not authorized by the trust. 55-56 V., c. 29, s. 363.

A period of speculation in real estate such as Canada has recently passed through is inseparable from conditions where persons contract to sell what they themselves have not title to, and for which they have not paid, and for which they may never pay. The losses which are being suffered by many buyers of land who have paid their money and are unable to obtain title or to secure return of the moneys paid show that our laws are defective in the obligations which they impose on those who sell under such circumstances. The purpose of a purchaser in paying money is to become the owner of the land which he buys. Until that purpose is accomplished, the purchaser should have an interest in the moneys which he has paid. At present the law gives him no interest, and when he cannot obtain title to lands purchased ihis only right is to a judgment for damages which will include the moneys paid. This course will always be expensive, but usually valueless. Our law at present treats these purchase moneys as belonging to the seller of lands, and imposes no corresponding duty to make use of them for the purpose for which they are paid, namely, to perfect title in the purchaser. Sometimes the moneys are squandered before the eyes of a purchaser who has no right to interfere, for he has no interest in the moneys, no matter what his misgivings may be. This Bill would impose a duty on such a seller of land to use the money in clearing up his own title, and .to hold in trust any moneys not so used until that end is accomplished. Until the vendor has title in himself, the purchaser would have an interest in any moneys which may be in the vendor's hands. The principle is not new, for where the title is held by the vendor the interest of the purchaser in the property being paid for is recognized. The statement in Halsbury's " Laws of England," vol. 28, p. 64, is as follows :
A person who has contracted to sell real pro-pertj to the purchaser is in a sense a trustee of it for the purchaser, but until the completion of the purchase he has a lien upon it for the payment of the purchase money. He has also a substantial and paramount interest in the property, and a right to protect that Interest, and an active right to assert that interest if anything is done in derogation of it.
This Bill would apply the same'principle to the converse case, and would impose a trust interest on behalf of a purchaser in the moneys paid where the interest could not be imposed on the lands.

member, and there is, no doubt, a good deal to be said in favour of the proposition.

Quite a number of those would have a great deal to he said in their favour if we should depart from that rule. Should we facilitate the passing of the Bill of the hon. member, I think it will be agreed that it would only be fair that those who have suggested other amendments should have an opportunity of submitting them, and, if amending legislation is to be passed, that there should be an opportunity of embodying in the Bill the amendments sought by these other parties, if they should be approved. My hon. friend the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) the other evening pressed upon us very strongly an amendment to the Criminal Code connected with the Copyright Act. I may say, therefore, that I would be disposed, with the understanding that by so doing we do not necessarily adopt the principle of the Bill, to allow this Bill to have its second reading, and after that I shall at a subsequent sitting move that it be referred to a committee together with such other suggested amendments to the Criminal Code as may come up.

speechtext:
Mr. W. F. MACLEAN (South York) moved the second reading of Bill No. 30, to amend the Railway Act. He said:
A year ago the Government brought in a Bill to amend the general Railway Act, and in it there was a clause placing the regulation of the capitalization of railway companies under the control of the Railway Commission. We have received no intima-

tion from the Government that they intend introducing legislation this session to amend the Railway Act, but I am convinced that the railway situation is such that if we do not re-introduce the whole of the proposed amending legislation, we ought to bring forward some of its more important clauses and have them put into law this session, particularly in view of the fact that the difficulties sought to he removed may be increased by neglect of Parliament to deal with the matter this session.
I have called the attention of this House time after time to the capitalization of one great company in Canada, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. I have endeavoured to point out that that company has been financing in an expensive way at the expense of the country, and especially at the expense of those who use the railway. I did suggest that we should have a law similar to that which they have in many of the states of the Union, providing that a company's capitalization shall be subject to regulation by a commission, which would see that any money raised for the benefit of the company is raised only because it is absolutely necessary, and in such a manner as to place the lightest burden upon the people who use the railway. The Canadian Pacific railway and other railways in this country have, so far as I can make out, conducted their financial operations in a manner expensive to those who use the road, and therefore I think it is high time that we should adopt the system which now prevails in New York State, thus providing that if a railway wishes to increase its capitalization it must show good reason for doing so and must show that the method it proposes to employ is one that is in the public interest.
There is a rumour in the press that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company intend to increase their capitalization, to divide the company, and to do other things that are, I think, largely in the interests of the shareholders rather than in the interests of the country. In this time when transportation is, as was stated here this afternoon of greatest importance, it is essential that the intention of the Government to brin^ the capitalization of railways under public control should be speedily carried out. If we neglect it this session something will he done in the meantime by the railway that will be against the public interest. We have taken over control of the Canadian Northern railway, and its capitalization is

now strictly within the control of this Parliament. Why should not that be the case with every other railway company that we have in Canada? As I said, there is a danger of the public interest being jeopardized by new legislation on the part of the Canadian Pacific railway and other roads. It is for the purpose of having these matters immediately placed under the Railway Commission and of preventing anything unfair to the public being done that I urge that this law should be adopted this session. There is no harm done to the railway if it be made to justify its new issues, and if it is shown that the plan which it proposes to follow is in the public interest there is no hardship in it.
The great trouble to-day throughout the world is improvident capitalization in connection with great corporations. The experience of the United States in connection with the Boston and Maine, the New York, New Haven and Hartford especially, the Rock Island and other railroads show that road after road has been ruined or injured by improvident capitalization; and, as a consequence, the people of the United States are now seeking to bring all of this capitalization under control. To show what improvident legislation will do in the way of capitalization one has only to look at the failures all over Canada, from ocean to ocean, in connection with over-capitalized companies. If you take the mergers that have taken place, if you look into the flotations that have been made, if you look into the way in which the great industries of ibis country have been over-capitalized and then put in a condition that they could not pay their interest or any dividends, and if you look at and realize the way they have been wrecked, you will find that over-capitalization is the cause of their trouble. A marvellous light has been thrown on this question of capitalization in the United States lately. A man named Henry Ford started a great automobile industry, beginning in a very small way. He succeeded in the operations of his company and he is to-day distributing $25,000,000 of the profits of his company among his employees. He is enabled to do it because there has been no water injected into that great company. You find company after company whose profits ought to be as large as Ford's; had they not to pay dividends on watered stock the owners would have been enabled to do as Ford has done and to pay out the profits of the company for the benefit of the workingman.

Anyone who professes to have the interests of labour at heart must admit that the only way to get fair treatment out of the great bulk of these corporations is to control their capitalization, put it down to the lowest possible amount and have it of a kind that bears least on those wdro are patrons of the proposition. If a company finance by issuing bonds say at 4 per cent instead of stock on which owners expect 10 per cent and if we stop this business of cutting melons we will overcome much of the trouble. It is not a legitimate proposition that a public company, holding a public franchise, should devote its time to cutting melons for the benefit of the shareholders; it should he devoting its main attention to the service of the public and there cannot he good and faithful service to the public where there is an enormous over-capitalization-and there are so many instances of it. Take all these outside flotations that are centered in Canada with franchises today in parts of the world. We have had scores and scores floated all over Canada, Mexicans, South Americans, and others. They have all been over capitaized, none of them have realized the promises of their promoters; the public served by the franchise have not had a good service and the people who have invested their capital have largely lost thereby. They have lost because we allowed this unfair capitalization to take place. It must he regulated. We have been promised in Parliament time after time that it would be regulated. We have had Ministers of Justice in this House who have said that it was not any concern of the public that they ought to be regulated,	but	all experience goes
to show	that you must regulate
capitalization in such a way as to bear least on the public. That is all I ask. I ask that the railways of this country, who have undertaken to solve the transportation problem of Canada shall do it on sound financial lines, on lines that will be approved of by the public and be in the public interest. The Government of the day have recognized this principle. They put it in a Bill which they introduced last session. That Bill was delayed. I do not see why it should be delayed now. I see the seriousness of the situation in regard to the war, but I also see the disturbance the war is causing to the transportation and the settlement of our West, and in trying to build the West up again and have it populated, we should let the people of the West and of Canada know that when we are creating corporations for the public we shall take power to regulate their capitalization. I say that is a reasonable thing and if we neglect to do it now some of these companies will get away from our jurisdiction and do whatever they wish before they come under the law7. If the Government will say that they did not quite see their way this session to go on with this legislation but they will give notice to the corporations that none of them will be allowed to deal with their capitalization until the general law can be passed, I might be satisfied to accept that and probably the country would be satisfied. I feel that I do not need to argue in favour of this proposition. The consensus of opinion is in favour of it. The effect of the clause that I have here tonight is a recognized Government measure of last session. Inasmuch as they are following on the lines of legislation in other countries I say that we ought to adopt it now and let every one know that hereafter undue inflation in connection with public franchises, and especially railways* will not be allowed.
A Bill was introduced in this House in connection with a steamship company a year or so ago. I opposed it and I gave as a reason then that there was a flotation proposition in it that was against the interests of the public. It was denied in a way, but what happened afterwards? They organized under the Companies Act and they did what they liked in connection with tneir flotations. It has been a great disappointment to the people who put their money into it. Our. object today, if we are to assist in the recuperation of Canada, in trying to regain our position after this war, will be to encourage and allow only sound financing in this country in connection with these companies. If we put an end for all time to this high financing and get them back to honest and fair measures, we shall be doing a lot to put this country in better shape. It will take this country and the mother country and every nation in Europe years to recover from the setback occasioned by the war, and nothing will so much prevent a recovery as unfair financing. I could go fully into that and give argument after argument, but it does not require it. It seems to me absolutely in the public interest that the high financing which takes place in connection with railways in this and other countries should cease. All these matters should be under the control of a public body and, following the lines of the Government Bill

of last session, my suggestion is to put these matters under the regulation of the Railway Commission.
The other clause of this Bill deals with a matter that largely affects the cities of Toronto and Montreal, and in fact the whole country. The clause is taken from the Government Bill of last session, and is to give power to the Railway Commission to make an order, if it sees fit, whereby a municipality can associate itself with a railway company that proposes to build a bridge within the municipality, in order that a joint bridge may be built for vehicular and steam traffic. That is a sound common-sense principle. In my own constituency the Canadian Pacific railway has built within the last two or three years two great bridges. The township council of York, through its council, approached the railway company and asked to be allowed to join in the building of the bridge so that a roadway might be made for the public. The railway company said they were ready to discuss the matter; but it was not discussed. Other great bridges are to be built in my constituency over ravines that the public wish to cross, and they would be prepared to pay a fair share of the cost if they had an opportunity of doing so. This clause is to give them that right. One of the members of the city of Montreal, when this matter was up in the Railway Committee a year ago, pointed out that it was of the greatest importance to the people of Montreal as also to people of other towns and ciues in the province of Quebec. I have seen members of the Railway Committee urge time after time that municipalities be given the right to join with the railways in building bridges. The Railway Commission would apportion the cost. Member after member from the West has brought up cases of this kind where people want a public roadway in connection with the bridges that are built across the rivers and ravines in their districts. In a number of cases the railways have of their own motion joined with the municipalities in giving such a public service bridge. The demand for this kind oi bridge is greatly increasing. The question is up in my constituency, and in the city of Toronto where the railways propose to build additional bridges over the great ravines that surround the city, and tnere is no reason why the city of Toronto and the municipality should not have the *right to join with the railway company in order to get a public roadway a? well as 
a railway bridge. These two things are in the public interest and are needed now and every day, and I see no reason why Parliament should not put these two clauses on the statute-book this year. It is for that purpose, because I think it is in the public interest, that I have introduced the Bill this session. I should like to have it read a second time, but would prefer to have seen it discussed in Committee of the 'Whole House and dealt with there; but as the Minister of Railways has moved that the previous Bill go to the Railway Committee I suppose, if the House sees fit, the same course will be taken with this Bill, and that I shall have to bring forward my arguments there. The need for this legislation is apparent to everybody, and it is more needed now than ever it was. It will 'help to meet the general transportation question, and the financing of the railways. It will help the settlement of the country, and give farmers better rates and better bridges to the towns, and Parliament will [DOT]have done something towards meeting conditions in this country. For that reason I move the second reading of this Bill.

At this late hour I shall only occupy the House for a moment or two. I quite agree with the object of the Bill and the remarks made *by the mover. I think the over-capitalization of our railways is one of the biggest difficulties that this Parliament will have to deal with in the future. If it were not for over-capitalization I do not think the different railways would be coming here before the Railway Commission on the 1st of March next to ask for an increase in railway rates. Nor would they need to increase the rates to pay handsome dividends *on their capitalization, at least on all the *money that went into their capitalization. There is no reason why we should not take this action. The country practically financed the Canadian Pacific railway, and certainly the Canadian Northern railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific, the three companies which own practically the whole mileage in Canada. As this Bill is exactly in accordance with what the Government undertook to do last year I trust the minister will see 'his way clear to accept and pass it this session. I see by the press that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company again proposes to ask for a large increase in their capitalization. As the hon. member for South York has pointed out, if not to-night, on some former occasion, if the money was borrowed on debentures at four per cent, it would not be necessary to

charge as high freight rates to pay that interest as the company has to do when it sells stock on what it now pays ten per cent, and on which I presume it expects to pay ten per cent in the future. There can be no harm in asking the railways to come before the board and make out their case. They can say how much money they want and how they propose to get it, and if they make out a reasonable case the Railway Commission would undoubtedly give them the authority they ask for. But if they can get money at four per cent instead of ten per cent, I think the Railway Commission would say to them that it was in the interests of the company, in the interest of its patrons, and of the farmers and producers and of everybody that used the road, that they should get the money on the cheapest basis and put it into the company instead of into the pockets of the shareholders. For these reasons I have much pleasure in seconding the motion for the second reading.

speechtext:
When a Bill
consolidating the Railway Act was -introduced last year, which embodied several new features, and among others the one that is expressed in the first section of the Bill introduced by the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean), it,was the intention of the Government at that time, and that intention was carried out, to give to all persons interested in the proposed amendment an opportunity of being heard. That was carried out last year by the constitution of a special committee of this House and a similar committee was appointed in the Senate in order that there might be economy of time in the discussion of the amendments. It was apprehended that a great many interests would desire to be heard before the committees,' and it was more convenient that the hearing should take place once for all. It had also the 'additional advantage that if the two committees conferred together and worked practically as one committee, although technically they were two committees, there would be a better opportunity of coming to a definite conclusion which would carry the judgment of both Houses of Parliament. The committees were so constituted, and I believe that considerable hearings were had. The report of the evidence has been placed before both Houses of Parliament. My hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) comes this year with this proposition which embodies one of the amendments that he alluded to, and he has supported it by reference to capitalization. As far as the Canadian Pacific railway, to which he has particularly alluded, is concerned, I am not especially aware of the affairs of the company, but I have a very strong impression that the capitalization is represented by solid cash put into the enterprise. I do not think that in respect of that railway it can be said that there is any portion of its stock which is not' represented by money actually expended. My hon. friend the member for York has advocated the view that if stock is issued it should be issued at or very nearly the figure which the stock from time to time commands on the market. It has been urged by different railway companies, par-
	-
ticularly by the one to which he alludes, that it would be impracticable to raise money in that way and for the reason, among others which have been urged, that no one could foresee the contingencies which might arise between the time that the figure was fixed and the time that people were called upon to subscribe to the stock. The event of tremendous importance which occurred six months ago is an indication that circumstances might arise which would make it impossible for a railway company to fix, without the possibilitv of an amendment or change, the figure at which its stock should be offered for subscription unless one were to contemplate the possibility of the absolute - failure of any subscription at all.
My hon. friend refers to the possibility of raising money in a way which will be more in the public interest than by the issuance of stock. All these matters are of course very proper for consideration by such a tribunal, if one should be established to supervise the issuing of stock or of debentures for the purpose of providing necessary capital in addition to that already provided. I think we should bear in mind what my hon. friend the member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) has said, if I gathered his meaning correctly, that is, that money for the building of railways in this country must be very largely provided from abroad; and in dealing with all these matters we must have regard to the consideration that capital will not come to us from abroad for that purpose or for any other purpose unless those who propose to invest it can do so under such conditions as will make the investment a safe and a reasonably remunerative one. I am aware that in several of the states a provision somewhat similar to this has been in force, although I am not sure that it goes precisely along the same lines. I understand -I do not know whether it is correct or not -that commissions in the United States have refused, even at the request of the company proposing to make the issue, to authorize that issue at a higher rate than par. That has been so represented to me, but I have not had an opportunity of investigating the question nor do I understand at the moment precisely the reason which would induce any commission to come to such a conclusion. What I have said, however, relates to matters that are very proper to be considered by the committee to which the Bill will be referred if the House should so decide, be-

cause it is the proposal of the Government, as my hon. friend has said, that the Bill should be referred to a committee for the purpose of giving an opportunity to those who may desire to be heard.
I have not had an opportunity of giving much consideration to the proposal which is embodied in the second section of the Bill, but I am bound to say that the impression which I gathered from the remarks of my hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean) and of my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) leads me to think that a proposal of that kind has a good deal	to	commend	it.	We have
not any money in this	country to
waste in the building of two bridges where one would be sufficient. It is necessary for us to do a great deal of construction of that kind in the vast territory which it is our duty to develop; and if by adding at small expense to .t railway bridge, a footway or a way for carriages under the conditions set forth in the Bill can be provided, it seems to me that the proposal is an eminently fair one and entirely reasonable. In fact if I remember correctly, the late Administration, on one occasion, when the Victoria bridge was being rebuilt, gave some assistance-I think it was the payment of a certain sum of money-so that in the reconstruction of the bridge a footway should be added.
